## 5 Subcubic Time Algorithm for Graphs with Bounded Integer Weights

In this section, we show how to improve the running time of $2$ FRP when we restrict the graphs to graphs with small integer edge weights and no negative cycles, providing proofs for Theorem 1.3 and Corollary 1.4.

### 5.1 General Approach and Intuitions

We first give some intuitions and high-level ideas of our algorithm.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be an $n$ -vertex directed graph with integer edge weights in $\{-M\ldots M\}$ and no negative cycles. Let $s$ be the source and $t$ be the target for our $2$ FRP instance. The general approach to our algorithm is to divide $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ into intervals of $g$ vertices each for a positive integer parameter $g=O(n)$ .55 5 For instance, we will set $g=n^{(\omega-1)/3}=O(n)$ when $M=O(1)$ . Let $I$ be one of the intervals, then we use $V(I)$ to denote the vertices inside the interval, and $E(I)$ to denote the edges inside the interval. The intervals are created in such a way that the last vertex in the previous interval is the first vertex in the next interval. Once we have created these intervals we can classify all the two-fault replacement paths queries to the following three cases: (1) only one failed edge is on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ , (2) both failed edges are on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ in the same interval, and (3) both failed edges are on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ in different intervals. Note that we don’t need to consider cases where neither of the failed edges is on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ as the original shortest path will exist in $G\setminus\{e_{1},e_{2}\}$ . Now, we can create three separate sub-algorithms that handle each of these cases, and combine them to get the overall $2$ FRP algorithm.

We will have a general precomputation step and some sub-algorithms will also have their own precomputation steps to compute any needed information that was not computed in the general precomputation step. Our approach to querying the length of the replacement path in all of the sub-algorithms is to construct a weighted auxiliary graph to aid with the query. To build one such auxiliary graph, we first determine a set of critical vertices that break down the replacement path into a series of subpaths between them. These vertices will form the vertex set of the auxiliary graph, and the edges in the auxiliary graph will represent subpaths between these vertices.

We say that the auxiliary graph encodes a subpath from $u$ to $v$ in $G\setminus\{e_{1},e_{2}\}$ if there is a path from $u$ to $v$ in the auxiliary graph with the same length as the subpath. We also say that an edge $(u,v)$ in the auxiliary graph encodes a subpath from $u$ to $v$ in $G\setminus\{e_{1},e_{2}\}$ if the weight of that edge equals the length of the subpath. We will show many of those subpaths are encoded in the auxiliary graph, and eventually, show that the $s$ - $t$ shortest path in $G\setminus\{e_{1},e_{2}\}$ is encoded. Thus, we can run a Single-Source Shortest Paths (SSSP) algorithm on the auxiliary graph to get the length of the shortest replacement path.

### 5.2 Precomputed Distances

In the general precomputation step and the precomputation steps specific to each sub-algorithm, we will use the SSRP algorithm from [GV20] that has the same running time as Zwick’s APSP algorithm for graphs with edge weights in $\{-M,\ldots,M\}$ and our algorithm for SSRP with a small set of targets from Lemma 3.3. In the precomputation steps and the query step, we will also use the near-linear time SSSP algorithm by Bernstein, Nanongkai and Wulff-Nilsen [BNWN22]. On $n$ -vertex dense graphs, their algorithm runs in $\tilde{O}(n^{2})$ time.

In this general precomputation step we compute sets of distances that will be needed for all three sub-algorithms:

- 1. Run SSSP and SSRP from $s$ in $G$ , and store the results.

- 2. Run SSSP and SSRP from $t$ in $\widehat{G}$ , where $\widehat{G}$ represents $G$ with the directions of all of its edges reversed, and store the results.

- 3. For each interval $I$ , create the graphs $G\setminus E(I)$ and $\widehat{G\setminus E(I)}$ , then: (a) Run SSSP and SSRP with target set $V(I)\cup\{t\}$ from $s$ in $G\setminus E(I)$ , and store the results. (b) Run SSSP and SSRP with target set $V(I)\cup\{s\}$ from $t$ in $\widehat{G\setminus E(I)}$ and store the results.

- 4. Run Zwick’s All-Pairs Shortest Paths algorithm [Zwi02] on the graph with all the edges of $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ removed and store the results.

Steps 1, 2 and 4 take $\tilde{O}(M^{1/(4-\omega)}n^{2+1/(4-\omega)})$ time, and each iteration of step 3 takes $\tilde{O}(Mn^{\omega}+M^{1/(4-\omega)}n^{1+1/(4-\omega)}g)$ time, so overall these pre-processing steps take $\tilde{O}(Mn^{\omega+1}/g+M^{1/(4-\omega)}n^{2+1/(4-\omega)})$ time. The space complexity of the stored results in this step is $\tilde{O}(n^{2})$ .

### 5.3 Only One Failed Edge on Original Shortest Path

First, we consider the case where only one of the failed edges is on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ . Let $e_{1}$ be the failed edge on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ , $I_{1}$ be the interval containing $e_{1}$ , and $e_{2}$ be the failed edge that is not on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ . Our auxiliary graph requires distances not computed in the general precomputation step of the algorithm, so we will have a precomputation step for this algorithm. During this precomputation step, we compute a single-fault DSO for $G\setminus\pi_{G}(s,t)$ . Using Chechik and Cohen’s DSO [CC20], the pre-processing time is $\tilde{O}(Mn^{2.8729})$ and the space is $\tilde{O}(n^{2.5})$ . If all edge weights are positive integers in $\{1,\ldots,M\}$ , we can instead use Gu and Ren’s DSO [GR21], which has $\tilde{O}(Mn^{2.5794})$ pre-processing time and $\tilde{O}(n^{2})$ size. Note that although Gu and Ren’s DSO has $\tilde{O}(n^{2})$ size, it could use $\tilde{O}(n^{2.4207})$ space during pre-processing [GR21].

Let $G^{\prime}$ be the auxiliary graph, and let its vertex set be $\{s,t\}\cup V(I_{1})$ . We will add edges in the following steps:

- 1. Add an edge from $s$ to $t$ with weight $d_{G\setminus E(I_{1})}(s,t,e_{2})$ .

- 2. For every $v\in V(I)$ , add an edge $(s,v)$ with weight $d_{G\setminus E(I_{1})}(s,v,e_{2})$ .

- 3. For every $v\in V(I)$ , add an edge $(v,t)$ with weight $d_{G\setminus E(I_{1})}(v,t,e_{2})$ .

- 4. Add all of the edges in $I_{1}$ that are not one of the two failed edges. Then, for every $u,v\in V(I_{1})$ , add the edge $(u,v)$ with weight $d_{G\setminus\pi_{G}(s,t)}(u,v,e_{2})$ .

Now we can run SSSP from $s$ in $G^{\prime}$ . Since there are $O(g)$ vertices in each interval, there are $O(g)$ vertices in $G^{\prime}$ , so building $G^{\prime}$ and running the query takes $\tilde{O}(g^{2})$ times.

#### Theorem 5.1.

$d_{G^{\prime}}(s,t)$ is equal to $d_{G\setminus\{e_{1},e_{2}\}}(s,t)$ .

#### Proof.

Here are two main cases for the shortest $s$ - $t$ path that avoids $e_{1}$ and $e_{2}$ : (1) the path does not use any edge in $E(I_{1})$ or (2) the path does use edges in $E(I_{1})$ . The path for the first case is encoded in $G^{\prime}$ via the edge added in step 1.

For the second case, let $P$ be a canonical replacement path. We know that the shortest path $P$ must use a vertex in $V(I_{1})$ . Let $u$ be the first vertex on the replacement path that is in $V(I_{1})$ , and $v$ be the last vertex on the replacement path that is in $V(I_{1})$ . Then, the replacement path can be broken down into three subpaths: (1) a subpath from $s$ to $u$ , (2) a subpath from $u$ to $v$ , and (3) a subpath from $v$ to $t$ . If $G^{\prime}$ encodes each of these subpaths for every possible value of $u$ and $v$ , and the replacement path does use edges in $E(I_{1})$ , then $\pi_{G^{\prime}}(s,t)$ will use the optimal choices for $u$ and $v$ , which will give us the length of the replacement path.

First, we will focus on the subpaths from $s$ to $u$ for all choices of $u$ . Since $u$ will be the first vertex in $V(I_{1})$ on the replacement path, this subpath will not use any edge in $E(I_{1})$ . Similarly, the subpaths from $v$ to $t$ will not use any edge in $E(I_{1})$ either, since $v$ is the last vertex in $V(I_{1})$ on the replacement path. All of the subpaths must also avoid $e_{2}$ , since it is a failed edge. Therefore, the edges added in steps 2 and 3 are sufficient to encode the $s$ - $u$ subpaths and $v$ - $t$ subpaths into $G^{\prime}$ .

Next, we will focus on the subpaths between $u$ and $v$ for all choices of $u$ and $v$ . If a canonical replacement path does travel between two vertices in $V(I_{1})$ , then it will not use any edge on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ outside of $I_{1}$ to do so, as that would prevent it from being canonical. For example, if the path between $u$ and $v$ reached a vertex $w$ in $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ before $I_{1}$ , then the replacement path should go directly from $s$ to $w$ , instead of going to $u$ first, because it is canonical. The mirror situation occurs if it touches a vertex after $I_{1}$ and cannot happen for similar reasons. Therefore, when traveling between two vertices in $V(I_{1})$ , the replacement path will only use edges in $E(I_{1})$ and edges not on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ . As a result, every $u$ - $v$ subpath can be broken into a series of smaller paths consisting of edges in $E(I_{1})$ and paths between vertices in $V(I_{1})$ that do not use any edge on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ . The edges in step 4 encode all of these smaller paths into $G^{\prime}$ , and as a result every $u$ - $v$ subpath is encoded in $G^{\prime}$ .

In total, $G^{\prime}$ encodes every possible subpath which the replacement path could be constructed from, so the shortest $s$ - $t$ path in $G^{\prime}$ can not be longer than the replacement path in $G\setminus\{e_{1},e_{2}\}$ . It is impossible for $d_{G^{\prime}}(s,t)$ to be smaller than $d_{G\setminus\{e_{1},e_{2}\}}(s,t)$ because all of the edges in $G^{\prime}$ have weights that correspond to the lengths of some paths that are present in $G\setminus\{e_{1},e_{2}\}$ . Therefore, $d_{G^{\prime}}(s,t)$ must be equal to $d_{G\setminus\{e_{1},e_{2}\}}(s,t)$ . $\Box$

### 5.4 Both Failed Edges on Original Shortest Path: Same Interval

Next, we will consider the case where both failed edges $e_{1},e_{2}$ are on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ in the same interval $I$ . We start by constructing the auxiliary graph for this query. Let $G^{\prime}$ be the auxiliary graph, and let its vertex set be $\{s,t\}\cup V(I)$ . We will add edges in the following steps:

- 1. Add an edge from $s$ to $t$ with weight $d_{G\setminus E(I)}(s,t)$ .

- 2. For every $v\in V(I)$ , add an edge $(s,v)$ with weight $d_{G\setminus E(I)}(s,v)$ .

- 3. For every $v\in V(I)$ , add an edge $(v,t)$ with weight $d_{G\setminus E(I)}(v,t)$ .

- 4. Add all of the edges in $I$ that are not one of the two failed edges. Then, for every $u,v\in V(I)$ , add an edge $(u,v)$ with weight $d_{G\setminus\pi_{G}(s,t)}(u,v)$ .

Now we can run SSSP from $s$ in $G^{\prime}$ . Since there are $O(g)$ vertices in each interval, there are $O(g)$ vertices in $G^{\prime}$ , so building $G^{\prime}$ and running the query takes $\tilde{O}(g^{2})$ time. All of the edge weights of $G^{\prime}$ were already calculated in the general precomputation step, so there is no additional precomputation step for this sub-algorithm.

#### Theorem 5.2.

$d_{G^{\prime}}(s,t)$ is equal to $d_{G\setminus\{e_{1},e_{2}\}}(s,t)$ .

#### Proof.

The proof for this case is similar to the proof of Theorem 5.1 since both only involve one interval $I$ on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ . As before, there are two main cases for the shortest $s$ - $t$ path that avoids $e_{1}$ and $e_{2}$ : (1) the path does not use any edge in $E(I)$ or (2) the path does use edges in $E(I)$ . The path for the first case is encoded in $G^{\prime}$ via the edge added in step 1.

For the second case, let $P$ be a canonical replacement path, let $u$ be the first vertex on $P$ that is in $V(I)$ , and let $v$ be the last vertex on $P$ that is in $V(I)$ . As before, $P$ can be broken down into a subpath from $s$ to $u$ , a subpath from $u$ to $v$ , and a subpath from $v$ to $t$ . If $G^{\prime}$ encodes each of these subpaths for every possible value of $u$ and $v$ , and $P$ does use edges in $E(I)$ , then $\pi_{G^{\prime}}(s,t)$ will use the optimal choices for $u$ and $v$ , which will give us the length of the replacement path.

First, we will focus on the subpaths from $s$ to $u$ for all choices of $u$ . Since $u$ will be the first vertex in $V(I)$ on $P$ , this subpath will not use any edge in $E(I)$ . Therefore, the edges added in step 2 encode these subpaths into $G^{\prime}$ . Similarly, the subpaths from $v$ to $t$ will also not use any edge in $E(I)$ , since $v$ is the last vertex in $V(I)$ on $P$ . Therefore, the edges added in step 3 encode these subpaths into $G^{\prime}$ .

Next, we will focus on the subpaths between $u$ and $v$ for all choices of $u$ and $v$ . Using similar reasoning to that presented in the previous proof, we find that when traveling between two vertices in $V(I)$ , $P$ will only use edges in $E(I)$ and edges not on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ . As a result, every $u$ - $v$ subpath can be broken into a series of smaller paths consisting of edges in $E(I)$ and paths between vertices in $V(I)$ that do not use any edge of $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ . The edges added in step 4 encode all of these smaller paths into $G^{\prime}$ , and as a result every $u$ - $v$ subpath is encoded in $G^{\prime}$ .

In total, $G^{\prime}$ encodes every possible subpath which the replacement path could be constructed from, so the shortest $s$ - $t$ path in $G^{\prime}$ can not be longer than the replacement path in $G\setminus\{e_{1},e_{2}\}$ . It is impossible for $d_{G^{\prime}}(s,t)$ to be smaller than $d_{G\setminus\{e_{1},e_{2}\}}(s,t)$ either because all of the edges in $G^{\prime}$ have weights that correspond to the lengths of some paths that are present in $G\setminus\{e_{1},e_{2}\}$ . Therefore, $d_{G^{\prime}}(s,t)$ must be equal to $d_{G\setminus\{e_{1},e_{2}\}}(s,t)$ . $\Box$

### 5.5 Both Failed Edges on Original Shortest Path: Different Intervals

Finally, we will consider the case where both failed edges are on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ but in two different intervals $I_{1}$ and $I_{2}$ , where $I_{1}$ comes first on the shortest path. Let the failed edge in $I_{1}$ be $e_{1}=(a_{1},b_{1})$ and the failed edge in $I_{2}$ be $e_{2}=(a_{2},b_{2})$ .

We use $l_{1}$ (resp. $l_{2}$ ) to denote the first vertex of $I_{1}$ (resp. $I_{2}$ ), and $r_{1}$ (resp. $r_{2}$ ) to denote the last vertex of $I_{1}$ (resp. $I_{2}$ ). For the purposes of this query algorithm we will divide the vertices in $I_{1}$ and $I_{2}$ into four groups as follows: $L_{1}$ contains every vertex in $I_{1}$ from $l_{1}$ to $a_{1}$ inclusively, $R_{1}$ contains every vertex in $I_{1}$ from $b_{1}$ to $r_{1}$ inclusively, $L_{2}$ contains every vertex in $I_{2}$ from $l_{2}$ to $a_{2}$ inclusively, and $R_{2}$ contains every vertex in $I_{2}$ from $b_{2}$ to $r_{2}$ inclusively.

*Figure 6: Some notations used in Section 5.5.*

For technical reasons, we will first show how to compute the distance of replacement paths that are good, which is defined as follows.

#### Definition 5.3.

A replacement path $\pi_{G\setminus\{e_{1},e_{2}\}}(s,t)$ is called bad if it contains a subpath from $u$ to $v$ where

- 1. $u\in L_{1}$ and $v\in R_{1}$ ;

- 2. the subpath contains no other vertices in $V(I_{1})\cup V(I_{2})\cup\{s,t\}$ ;

- 3. and the subpath uses some edge on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ .

All other replacement paths are called good.

Clearly, if we reverse the directions of all the edges, switch the roles of $s$ and $t$ , and keep the same intervals in an algorithm that works for good replacement paths, the algorithm can work for replacement paths that are reversely good, which is more formally defined as follows.

#### Definition 5.4.

A replacement path $\pi_{G\setminus\{e_{1},e_{2}\}}(s,t)$ is called reversely bad if it contains a subpath from $u$ to $v$ where

- 1. $u\in L_{2}$ and $v\in R_{2}$

- 2. the subpath contains no other vertices in $V(I_{1})\cup V(I_{2})\cup\{s,t\}$

- 3. and the subpath uses some edge on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ .

All other replacement paths are called reversely good.

Our next lemma shows that a canonical replacement path is either good or reversely good, thus allowing us to focus on good and canonical replacement path since we can take care of the reversely good replacement paths by running the same algorithm for good replacement paths on $\widehat{G}$ with the roles of $s$ and $t$ switched.

#### Lemma 5.5.

Let $P$ be a canonical replacement path from $s$ to $t$ avoiding $e_{1}$ and $e_{2}$ , then $P$ is either good or reversely good.

#### Proof.

Assume for the sake of contradiction that $P$ is both bad and reversely bad. By the definitions, we can find $u_{1}\in L_{1}$ and $v_{1}\in R_{1}$ on $P$ such that the $u_{1}$ - $v_{1}$ subpath does not use any other vertices in $V(I_{1})\cup V(I_{2})\cup\{s,t\}$ while it uses some edge on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ . Also, we can find $u_{2}\in L_{2}$ and $v_{2}\in R_{2}$ such that the $u_{2}$ - $v_{2}$ subpath does not use any other vertices in $V(I_{1})\cup V(I_{2})\cup\{s,t\}$ while it uses some edge on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ .

Since $P$ is canonical, the $u_{1}$ - $v_{1}$ subpath must not use any edge before $e_{1}$ or after $e_{2}$ on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ . Also, it does not use any other vertices in $V(I_{1})\cup V(I_{2})\cup\{s,t\}$ , so it must not use any edge on $I_{1}$ or $I_{2}$ either. Therefore, the edge $(x,y)$ on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ that it uses must be after $I_{1}$ and before $I_{2}$ . Also, $u_{2}$ must appear later than $u_{1}$ and $v_{1}$ on $P$ , since the $s$ - $u_{1}$ subpath should exactly be $\pi_{G}(s,u_{1})$ by the assumption that $P$ is canonical and the $u_{1}$ - $v_{1}$ subpath does not use any other vertices in $V(I_{1})\cup V(I_{2})\cup\{s,t\}$ . However, since $P$ is canonical, once it reaches $x$ , it should head directly to $u_{2}$ using edges on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ instead of going to $v_{1}$ , a contradiction. $\Box$

From now on, we can focus on computing the lengths of good replacement paths.

Our auxiliary graph will require distances that were not computed in the general precomputation step, so we will have a precomputation step for this sub-algorithm. The precomputation step is as follows:

- 1. Run Lemma 3.2 to compute $f(v,u)=d_{G\setminus\pi_{G}(s,u)\setminus\pi_{G}(v,t)}(v,u)$ for all $u,v\in V(\pi_{G}(s,t))$ such that $u$ comes before $v$ on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ and store the results. Here, we use $\pi_{G}(s,u)$ to denote the subpath from $s$ to $u$ on the path $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ ; similarly, we use $\pi_{G}(v,t)$ to denote the subpath from $v$ to $t$ on the path $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ .

- 2. For each interval $I$ , create the graphs $G\setminus E(I)$ and $\widehat{G\setminus E(I)}$ , then: (a) Run SSRP with target set $V(I)\cup\{s,t\}$ from the last vertex in $V(I)$ in $G\setminus E(I)$ and store the results for all intervals $I$ . (b) Run SSRP with target set $V(I)\cup\{s,t\}$ from the first vertex in $V(I)$ in $\widehat{G\setminus E(I)}$ and store the results for all intervals $I$ .

Step 1 takes $\tilde{O}(M^{1/3}n^{2+\omega/3})$ time and each iteration of step 2 takes $\tilde{O}(Mn^{\omega}+M^{1/(4-\omega)}n^{1+1/(4-\omega)}g)$ time, so overall the precomputation step of this sub-algorithm takes $\tilde{O}(Mn^{\omega+1}/g+M^{1/(4-\omega)}n^{2+1/(4-\omega)}+M^{1/3}n^{2+\omega/3})$ time. By Lemma 3.2, we can improve the third term to $\tilde{O}(M^{0.3544}n^{2.7778})$ using rectangular matrix multiplication. The space complexity is again $\tilde{O}(n^{2})$ .

Let the auxiliary graph be called $G^{\prime}$ and let its vertex set be $\{s,t\}\cup V(I_{1})\cup V(I_{2})$ . We will add edges to $G^{\prime}$ in the following steps:

- 1. Add an edge from $s$ to $t$ with weight $\min\left\{d_{G\setminus E(I_{1})}(s,t,e_{2}),d_{G\setminus E(I_{2})}(s,t,e_{1}))\right\}$ .

- 2. Add every edge in $E(I_{1})$ other than $e_{1}$ , and every edge in $E(I_{2})$ other than $e_{2}$ .

- 3. Add an edge from $s$ to $l_{1}$ with weight $d_{G}(s,l_{1})$ , an edge from $r_{2}$ to $t$ with weight $d_{G}(r_{2},t)$ , and an edge from $r_{1}$ to $l_{2}$ with weight $d_{G}(r_{1},l_{2})$ .

- 4. For all $v\in L_{1}\cup R_{1}$ , add an edge from $s$ to $v$ with weight $d_{G\setminus E(I_{1})}(s,v,e_{2})$ and add an edge from $v$ to $t$ with weight $d_{G\setminus E(I_{1})}(v,t,e_{2})$ .

- 5. For all $v\in L_{2}\cup R_{2}$ , add an edge from $s$ to $v$ with weight $d_{G\setminus E(I_{2})}(s,v,e_{1})$ and add an edge from $v$ to $t$ with weight $d_{G\setminus E(I_{2})}(v,t,e_{1})$ .

- 6. For every $(u,v)\in R_{1}\times L_{2}$ , add an edge from $v$ to $u$ with weight $d_{G\setminus\pi_{G}(s,u)\setminus\pi_{G}(v,t)}(v,u)=f(v,u)$ .

- 7. For every $v\in R_{1}$ , add an edge from $r_{1}$ to $v$ with weight $d_{G\setminus E(I_{1})}(r_{1},v,e_{2})$ .

- 8. For every $v\in L_{2}$ , add an edge from $v$ to $l_{2}$ with weight $d_{G\setminus E(I_{2})}(v,l_{2},e_{1})$ .

- 9. For every $u,v\in V(I_{1})\cup V(I_{2})\cup\{s,t\}$ , add an edge from $u$ to $v$ with weight $d_{G\setminus\pi_{G}(s,t)}(u,v)$ .

Now we can run SSSP from $s$ in $G^{\prime}$ . Since there are $O(g)$ vertices in each interval, there are $O(g)$ vertices in $G^{\prime}$ , so building $G^{\prime}$ and running the query takes $\tilde{O}(g^{2})$ time. Each edge weight of $G^{\prime}$ can be computed in $O(1)$ time due to the general precomputation step and this sub-algorithm’s own precomputation step. We will show the following theorem.

#### Theorem 5.6.

$d_{G^{\prime}}(s,t)$ is equal to $d_{G\setminus\{e_{1},e_{2}\}}(s,t)$ as long as one of the canonical replacement paths is good.

In the following, let $P$ be a canonical and good shortest path from $s$ to $t$ in $G\setminus\{e_{1},e_{2}\}$ . We will first show the following two simple lemmas that will be used multiple times later.

#### Lemma 5.7.

Let $u$ , $v$ , and $w$ be vertices both on $P$ and in $G^{\prime}$ such that $u$ comes before $v$ on $P$ and $v$ comes before $w$ on $P$ . If the subpath from $u$ to $v$ of $P$ is encoded in $G^{\prime}$ , and the subpath from $v$ to $w$ of $P$ is encoded in $G^{\prime}$ , then the subpath from $u$ to $w$ of $P$ is encoded in $G^{\prime}$ .

#### Proof.

Due to the order of the vertices on $P$ , the length of the subpath from $u$ to $w$ can be written as $d_{G\setminus\{e_{1},e_{2}\}}(u,v)+d_{G\setminus\{e_{1},e_{2}\}}(v,w)$ . Since the $u$ - $v$ subpath is encoded in $G^{\prime}$ , there is a path in $G^{\prime}$ from $u$ to $v$ with weight $d_{G\setminus\{e_{1},e_{2}\}}(u,v)$ , and since the $v$ - $w$ subpath is encoded in $G^{\prime}$ , there is a path in $G^{\prime}$ from $v$ to $w$ with weight $d_{G\setminus\{e_{1},e_{2}\}}(v,w)$ . Therefore, there is a path in $G^{\prime}$ from $u$ to $w$ with weight $d_{G\setminus\{e_{1},e_{2}\}}(u,v)+d_{G\setminus\{e_{1},e_{2}\}}(v,w)$ , so the subpath from $u$ to $w$ is encoded in $G^{\prime}$ . $\Box$

We say that a subpath between two vertices $u$ and $v$ on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ moves forward if $u$ comes before $v$ on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ , and backward if $u$ comes after $v$ on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ .

#### Lemma 5.8.

There is no subpath of $P$ which moves backward to a vertex before $e_{1}$ , and there is no subpath of $P$ which moves backward from a vertex after $e_{2}$ .

#### Proof.

For any vertex $u$ on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ before $e_{1}$ , the subpath of $P$ from $s$ to $u$ is the same as the subpath of $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ from $s$ to $u$ , since $P$ is canonical. Therefore, it is impossible for there to be a subpath of $P$ that moves backward to $u$ as this would imply that the $s$ - $u$ subpath of $P$ is different from the $s$ - $u$ subpath of $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ .

Similarly, for any vertex $v$ on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ after $e_{2}$ , the subpath of $P$ from $v$ to $t$ is the same as the subpath of $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ from $v$ to $t$ . Therefore, it is impossible for there to be a subpath of $P$ that moves backward from $v$ as this would imply that the $v$ - $t$ subpath of $P$ is different from the $v$ - $t$ subpath of $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ . $\Box$

Using Lemma 5.7 and Lemma 5.8 as basic tools, we can proceed to the main proofs. The general strategy in this proof is an inductive approach. Suppose we have already showed that $G^{\prime}$ encodes the $s$ - $u$ subpath of $P$ for some $u$ , and $v$ is the first vertex after $u$ in $P$ that belongs to some subset of vertices $U\subseteq V(G^{\prime})$ . We will show that $G^{\prime}$ also encodes the $s$ - $v$ subpath of $P$ . We break down all cases to several lemmas depending on where $u$ is in the graph $G^{\prime}$ . The subset $U$ could be different in different lemmas, but it is essential that the set $U$ contains the vertex $t$ .

#### Lemma 5.9.

Let $u$ be the first vertex in $V(I_{1})\cup V(I_{2})\cup\{t\}$ on $P$ , then $G^{\prime}$ encodes the subpath from $s$ to $u$ on $P$ .

#### Proof.

We break down the cases depending on where $u$ is.

Suppose $u\in V(I_{1})$ . The subpath is encoded since we added the edge $(s,u)$ with weight $d_{G\setminus E(I_{1})}(s,u,e_{2})$ in step 4. It is sufficient since $u$ is the first vertex on $P$ in $V(I_{1})$ , so the $s$ to $u$ subpath will not use any edge in $E(I_{1})$ . Thus the subpath will exist in $G\setminus(E(I_{1})\cup\{e_{2}\})$ .

Similarly, suppose $u\in V(I_{2})$ , then the subpath is encoded since we added the edge $(s,u)$ with weight $d_{G\setminus E(I_{2})}(s,u,e_{1})$ in step 5. It is sufficient since $u$ is the first vertex on $P$ in $V(I_{2})$ , so the $s$ to $u$ subpath will not use any edge in $E(I_{2})$ . Thus the subpath will exist in $G\setminus(E(I_{2})\cup\{e_{1}\})$ .

Suppose $u=t$ , then the edge from $s$ to $t$ with weight $d_{G\setminus E(I_{1})}(s,t,e_{2})$ added in step 1 encodes the subpath since in this case $P$ does not contain any vertex in $V(I_{1})\cup V(I_{2})$ . $\Box$

#### Lemma 5.10.

Let $u\in L_{1}$ be a vertex on $P$ . Let $v$ be the first vertex after $u$ in $V(I_{1})\cup L_{2}\cup\{t\}$ on $P$ . Suppose $G^{\prime}$ encodes the subpath from $s$ to $u$ on $P$ , then $G^{\prime}$ encodes the subpath from $s$ to $v$ as well.

#### Proof.

We break down the cases depending on where $v$ is.

Suppose $v\in L_{1}$ . When moving within $L_{1}$ , the replacement path can move either forward or backward, as defined previously. The best way to move forward within $L_{1}$ is to follow the edges on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ , so by adding the edges in $E(I_{1})\setminus\{e_{1}\}$ in step 2 we are able to encode the $u$ to $v$ subpath into $G^{\prime}$ . By Lemma 5.7, $G^{\prime}$ also encodes the $s$ - $v$ subpath. $P$ will never move backward to a vertex in $L_{1}$ , as shown in Lemma 5.8.

Suppose $v\in R_{1}$ .66 6 This is the case where we need to assume $P$ is good. If the input graph doesn’t have negative edges, then we can afford to compute a full SSRP from $s$ in $G\setminus E(I_{2})$ instead of an SSRP with a small target set, and thus this case can be handled similarly to the next case by using $d_{G\setminus E(I_{2})}(s,v,e_{1})$ . For this reason, our proof can be simplified for graphs with edge weights in $\{1,\ldots,M\}$ . The $u$ - $v$ subpath cannot contain any vertex in $\{s\}\cup R_{2}$ by Lemma 5.8, and cannot contain any vertex (other than $u$ and $v$ ) in $V(I_{1})\cup L_{2}\cup\{t\}$ by definition of $v$ . Thus, the $u$ - $v$ subpath does not contain any other vertex in $V(I_{1})\cup V(I_{2})\cup\{s,t\}$ . Since $P$ is good, the $u$ - $v$ subpath does not use any edge on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ . Thus the $u$ - $v$ subpath is encoded by the edges added in step 9. Since the $s$ - $u$ and $u$ - $v$ subpaths are both encoded, $G^{\prime}$ encodes the $s$ - $v$ subpath by Lemma 5.7.

Suppose $v\in L_{2}$ . In this case, we will directly prove that $G^{\prime}$ encodes the $s$ to $v$ subpath. Since $P$ is canonical, the subpath from $s$ to $u$ must use edges on the $s$ - $u$ subpath on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ . Thus, the $s$ - $u$ subpath does not use any edge in $E(I_{2})$ . Since $v$ is the first vertex after $u$ in $V(I_{1})\cup L_{2}$ and $u$ is in $L_{1}$ , the $u$ - $v$ subpath can not use any edge in $E(I_{2})$ before $e_{2}$ as that would make it so that $v$ is not the first vertex after $u$ that is in $V(I_{1})\cup L_{2}$ . In addition, the $u$ - $v$ subpath can not use any edge after $e_{2}$ in $E(I_{2})$ by Lemma 5.8. Therefore, the $u$ - $v$ subpath can not use any edge in $E(I_{2})$ , so the $s$ - $v$ subpath does not use any edge in $E(I_{2})$ , meaning that it will be present in $G\setminus(E(I_{2})\cup\{e_{1}\})$ . Therefore, the edge from $s$ to $v$ with weight $d_{G\setminus E(I_{2})}(s,v,e_{1})$ added in step 5 encodes the $s$ - $v$ subpath.

Finally, suppose $v=t$ . The $u$ - $v$ subpath does not use any vertex in $V(I_{1})$ other than $u$ , so it does not use any edge in $E(I_{1})$ . It means that the $u$ - $v$ subpath will be present in $G\setminus(E(I_{1})\cup\{e_{2}\})$ , so the edges added in step 5 encode the $u$ - $v$ subpath into $G^{\prime}$ . $\Box$

#### Lemma 5.11.

Let $u\in R_{1}$ be a vertex on $P$ . Let $v$ be the first vertex after $u$ in $V(I_{1})\cup L_{2}\cup\{t\}$ on $P$ . Suppose $G^{\prime}$ encodes the subpath from $s$ to $u$ in $P$ , then $G^{\prime}$ encodes the subpath from $s$ to $v$ as well.

#### Proof.

We break down the cases depending on where $v$ is. Here, we will prove that $G^{\prime}$ encodes the $u$ to $v$ subpath, which will imply that $G^{\prime}$ encodes the $s$ to $v$ subpath by Lemma 5.7.

First, $v$ cannot be in $L_{1}$ since $P$ can not move backward to a vertex in $L_{1}$ by Lemma 5.8.

Suppose $v\in R_{1}$ , and $v$ is after $u$ on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ . The best way to move forward within $R_{1}$ is to follow the edges in $E(I_{1})\setminus\{e_{1}\}$ , which are added in step 2, so the $u$ - $v$ subpath is encoded in $G^{\prime}$ .

Suppose $v\in R_{1}$ , and $v$ is before $u$ on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ . Assume that $u$ is not $r_{1}$ . In this case, the $u$ - $v$ subpath cannot use any edge before $e_{1}$ or after $e_{2}$ on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ by Lemma 5.8. It cannot use any edge after $u$ and before $e_{2}$ because otherwise, since $P$ is canonical, it must use the vertex immediately after $u$ on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ , contradicting to the assumption that $v$ is the first vertex after $u$ in $V(I_{1})\cup L_{2}\cup\{t\}$ . It cannot use any edge after $e_{1}$ and before $u$ since $v$ is the first vertex after $u$ in $V(I_{1})$ on path $P$ . Therefore, the $u$ - $v$ subpath does not use any edge on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ . Thus, the edge from $u$ to $v$ with weight $d_{G\setminus\pi_{G}(s,t)}(u,v)$ added in step 9 encodes the $u$ - $v$ subpath for this case. Now, we assume that $u=r_{1}$ . In this scenario, the $u$ - $v$ subpath can not use any edge in $E(I_{1})$ since $v$ is the first vertex after $u$ in $V(I_{1})$ . Therefore, the edge from $r_{1}$ to $v$ with weight $d_{G\setminus E(I_{1})}(r_{1},v,e_{2})$ added in step 7 encodes the $u$ - $v$ subpath for this case.

Suppose $v\in L_{2}$ . Since $P$ is canonical, it must be the case that $u=r_{1}$ and $b=l_{2}$ . Therefore, the edge between $r_{1}$ and $l_{2}$ added in step 3 encodes the $u$ - $v$ subpath into $G^{\prime}$ .

Finally, suppose $v=t$ . The $u$ - $v$ subpath won’t use any edge in $E(I_{1})$ because it does not use any vertex in $V(I_{1})$ other than $u$ . It means that the $u$ - $v$ subpath will be present in $G\setminus(E(I_{1})\cup\{e_{2}\})$ , so the edge from $u$ to $t$ with weight $d_{G\setminus E(I_{1})}(u,t,e_{2})$ added in step 5 encodes the $u$ - $v$ subpath. $\Box$

#### Lemma 5.12.

Let $u\in L_{2}$ be a vertex on $P$ . Let $v$ be the first vertex after $u$ in $V(I_{1})\cup L_{2}\cup\{t\}$ on $P$ . Suppose $G^{\prime}$ encodes the subpath from $s$ to $u$ in $P$ , then $G^{\prime}$ encodes the subpath from $s$ to $v$ as well.

#### Proof.

We break down the cases depending on where $v$ is. Here, (for all but the last case) we will prove that $G^{\prime}$ encodes the $u$ to $v$ subpath, which will imply that $G^{\prime}$ encodes the $s$ to $v$ subpath by Lemma 5.7.

First, $v$ cannot be in $L_{1}$ since $P$ can not move backward to a vertex in $L_{1}$ by Lemma 5.8.

Suppose $v\in R_{1}$ . Since $v$ is the first vertex after $u$ in $R_{1}\cup L_{2}$ , the $u$ - $v$ subpath does not use any edge in $E(I_{1})$ after $e_{1}$ or any edge in $E(I_{2})$ before $e_{2}$ . In addition, the $u$ - $v$ subpath can not use any edge on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ before $e_{1}$ or after $e_{2}$ by Lemma 5.8. Overall, the $u$ - $v$ subpath lies completely in the graph $G\setminus\pi_{G}(s,r_{1})\setminus\pi_{G}(l_{2},t)\subseteq G\setminus\pi_{G}(s,v)\setminus\pi_{G}(u,t)$ . By the optimality of $P$ , the length of the $u$ - $v$ subpath equals $d_{G\setminus\pi_{G}(s,v)\setminus\pi_{G}(u,t)}(u,v)=f(u,v)$ . Thus, the edge from $u$ to $v$ with weight $f(u,v)$ added in step 6 encodes the $u$ - $v$ subpath.

Suppose $v\in L_{2}$ , and $v$ is after $u$ on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ . The best way to move forward within $L_{2}$ is to follow the edges on $E(I_{2})\setminus\{e_{2}\}$ , which are added in step 2, so the $u$ - $v$ subpath is encoded in $G^{\prime}$ .

Suppose $v\in L_{2}$ , and $v$ is before $u$ on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ . Assume that $v$ is not $l_{2}$ . In this case, the $u$ - $v$ subpath cannot use any edge before $e_{1}$ or after $e_{2}$ on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ by Lemma 5.8. It cannot use any edge after $e_{1}$ and before $v$ on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ because otherwise, since $P$ is canonical, the vertex right before $v$ on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ is also used, contradicting to the assumption that $v$ is the first vertex after $u$ in $V(I_{1})\cup L_{2}\cup\{t\}$ . It cannot use any edge after $v$ and before $e_{2}$ on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ since $v$ is the first vertex after $u$ in $V(I_{1})\cup L_{2}\cup\{t\}$ on path $P$ . Therefore, the $u$ - $v$ subpath does not use any edge on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ . Thus, the edge from $u$ to $v$ with weight $d_{G\setminus\pi_{G}(s,t)}(u,v)$ added in step 9 encodes the $u$ - $v$ subpath for this case. Now, we assume that $v=l_{2}$ . In this scenario, the $u$ - $v$ subpath can not use any edge in $E(I_{2})$ since $v$ is the first vertex after $u$ in $V(I_{1})\cup L_{2}\cup\{t\}$ . Therefore, the edge from $u$ to $l_{2}$ with weight $d_{G\setminus E(I_{2})}(u,l_{2},e_{1})$ added in step 8 encodes the $u$ - $v$ subpath for this case.

Finally, suppose $v=t$ . This case is slightly more complicated.77 7 For graphs with only positive edge weights this case can also be simplified by using $d_{G\setminus E(I_{1})}(u,t,e_{2})$ from full SSRP computations instead of SSRP with small target sets. First, by Lemma 5.8, the $u$ - $t$ subpath cannot contain any vertex on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ before $e_{1}$ . Also, by definition of $v$ , it cannot contain any vertex in $R_{1}$ or $L_{2}$ either. We further divide this case based on which vertices this subpath contains.

- 1. The subpath contains some vertex $w$ after $r_{1}$ and before $l_{2}$ on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ . In this case, the $s$ - $u$ subpath cannot contain any vertex $x$ in $R_{1}$ since otherwise the canonical path $P$ should move directly from $x$ to $w$ instead of going to $u$ first. The $u$ - $t$ subpath cannot contain any vertex $x$ in $R_{1}$ either as argued previously. Thus, the whole path $P$ does not contain any vertex in $R_{1}$ . If $P$ also doesn’t contain any vertex in $L_{1}$ , then $P$ doesn’t contain any vertex or edge in $I_{1}$ , so the $s$ - $t$ path is encoded by $d_{G\setminus E(I_{1})}(s,t,e_{2})$ added in step 1. If $P$ contains some vertex in $L_{1}$ , let $y$ be the last of them. The $s$ - $y$ subpath is encoded by the edges $d_{G}(s,l_{1})$ and the edges $E(I_{1})\setminus\{e_{1}\}$ , which were added in step 3 and 2 respectively. The $y$ - $t$ subpath thus doesn’t contain any edge in $E(I_{1})$ , so it is encoded by $d_{G\setminus E(I_{1})}(y,t,e_{2})$ added in step 4. Thus, the $s$ - $t$ subpath is encoded by Lemma 5.7.

- 2. The subpath doesn’t contain any vertex after $r_{1}$ and before $l_{2}$ , but contains some vertex in $R_{2}$ . Let $w$ be the first vertex in $R_{2}$ on this subpath. By the assumption and previous discussions, the $u$ - $w$ subpath cannot contain any edge before $e_{2}$ on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ ; it cannot contain any edge after $e_{2}$ on $E(I_{2})$ because $w$ is the first vertex in $R_{2}$ ; it cannot contain any edge after $I_{2}$ by Lemma 5.8. Thus, the $u$ - $w$ subpath doesn’t contain any edge on $\pi_{G}(s,t)$ and thus is encoded by $d_{G\setminus\pi_{G}(s,t)}(u,w)$ added in step 9. The $w$ - $t$ subpath is clearly encoded by edges $E(I_{2})\setminus\{e_{2}\}$ and the distance $d_{G}(r_{2},t)$ added in step 2 and step 3 respectively. Thus, $G^{\prime}$ encodes the $u$ - $t$ subpath by Lemma 5.7. Since we assume that $G^{\prime}$ encodes the $s$ - $u$ subpath, it also encodes the $s$ - $t$ subpath.

- 3. Finally, we assume the subpath doesn’t contain any vertex in $R_{2}$ . These three cases cover all possibilities. In this case, the $u$ - $t$ subpath does not use any edge in $E(I_{2})$ , meaning it will be present in $G\setminus(E(I_{2})\cup\{e_{1}\})$ , so the edge from $u$ to $t$ with weight $d_{G\setminus E(I_{2})}(u,t,e_{2})$ added in step 5 encodes the $u$ - $v$ subpath.

$\Box$

#### Lemma 5.13.

Let $u\in R_{2}$ be a vertex on $P$ . Let $v$ be the first vertex after $u$ in $R_{2}\cup\{t\}$ on $P$ . Suppose $G^{\prime}$ encodes the subpath from $s$ to $u$ in $P$ , then $G^{\prime}$ encodes the subpath from $s$ to $v$ as well.

#### Proof.

Suppose $v\in R_{2}$ . By Lemma 5.8, $u$ can only move forward to $v$ . The best way to move forward within $R_{2}$ is to follow the edges in $E(I_{2})\setminus\{e_{2}\}$ , which are added in step 2, so the $u$ - $v$ subpath is encoded in $G^{\prime}$ .

If $v=t$ , then since $P$ is canonical, $u$ must equal to $r_{2}$ , and the $u$ - $v$ subpath is encoded by the edge from $r_{2}$ to $t$ added in step 3. $\Box$

Now, we can prove Theorem 5.6:

#### Proof of Theorem 5.6.

Let $P$ be a good canonical shortest path from $s$ to $t$ in $G\setminus\{e_{1},e_{2}\}$ . We will show longer and longer prefixes of $P$ are encoded in $G^{\prime}$ and finally that $P$ is encoded in $G^{\prime}$ .

Initially, we set $u=s$ and clearly the subpath from $s$ to $u$ is encoded in $G^{\prime}$ . Now depending on where $u$ is, we can apply one of Lemma 5.9, Lemma 5.10, Lemma 5.11, Lemma 5.12 and Lemma 5.13. Using those lemmas, we find a vertex $v$ on $P$ after $u$ in a certain subset of vertices $U\subseteq V(G^{\prime})$ . The subset $U$ can be different depending on which lemma we are applying, but $U$ always contains $t$ , so we can always find such a vertex $v$ . By applying the corresponding lemma, and using the inductive assumption that $G^{\prime}$ encodes the $s$ to $u$ subpath, we obtain that $G^{\prime}$ encodes the $s$ to $v$ subpath. Thus, we could set $u$ to $v$ and keep applying the lemmas. Eventually $u$ will be set to $t$ .

We have shown that $G^{\prime}$ encodes $P$ , so the shortest $s$ - $t$ path in $G^{\prime}$ can not be longer than the replacement path in $G\setminus\{e_{1},e_{2}\}$ . It is impossible for $d_{G^{\prime}}(s,t)$ to be smaller than $d_{G\setminus\{e_{1},e_{2}\}}(s,t)$ because all of the edges in $G^{\prime}$ have weights that correspond to the lengths of some paths that are present in $G\setminus\{e_{1},e_{2}\}$ . Therefore, $d_{G^{\prime}}(s,t)$ must be equal to $d_{G\setminus\{e_{1},e_{2}\}}(s,t)$ . $\Box$

In total, the running time for the general precomputation phase and the precomputation phase of each sub-algorithm is $\tilde{O}(Mn^{\omega+1}/g+M^{1/(4-\omega)}n^{2+1/(4-\omega)}+M^{1/3}n^{2+\omega/3}+Mn^{2.8729})$ . The fourth term dominates the second and third term, so the pre-processing time simplifies to $\tilde{O}(Mn^{\omega+1}/g+Mn^{2.8729})$ . The space complexity is $\tilde{O}(n^{2.5})$ , where the space of the DSO is the bottleneck.

If all edge weights are positive, the pre-processing time can be improved to $\tilde{O}(Mn^{\omega+1}/g+M^{1/(4-\omega)}\allowbreak n^{2+1/(4-\omega)}+M^{1/3}n^{2+\omega/3}+Mn^{2.5794})$ . The third term can be improved to $\tilde{O}(M^{0.3544}n^{2.7778})$ using rectangular matrix multiplication by Lemma 3.2. Note that the second term is always dominated by the third term or the fourth term, so the pre-processing time simplifies to $\tilde{O}(Mn^{\omega+1}/g+M^{0.3544}n^{2.7778}+Mn^{2.5794})$ . The space complexity is $\tilde{O}(n^{2})$ .

The query time is $\tilde{O}(g^{2})$ in both cases, since we always run the near-linear time SSSP algorithm [BNWN22] on an auxiliary graph with $O(g)$ vertices. $\Box$

We can easily obtain our algorithm for $2$ FRP from Theorem 1.3 by setting the parameter appropriately. Recall Corrollary 1.4:
