The second step is by linearity of expectation. The third step is by definition of $\I_{q}$ .

Note that $\rho(*)=1-\frac{p_{-}}{2}-\frac{p_{+}}{2}=\frac{1}{2}\pm o(1)$ . Because $\I(f)\geq cn$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\rho^{\otimes[n]}}\I_{q}(f_{s})\geq(2c\pm o(1))n. $$

That is, $f_{s}$ has expected $q$ -biased total influence at least $(2c\pm o(1))n$ .

#### 4.4.3 Step 3b

We prove the following lemma, which essentially says that adaptive exact queries in Phase 3 can only decrease the $q$ -biased total influence $\I_{q}$ by a certain amount. In the following, recall the definition of $f_{t}$ for a Boolean function $f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}$ and $t\in\{0,1,*\}^{n}$ is $f$ where we restrict all input coordinates $i$ with $t_{i}\neq*$ to be equal to $t_{i}$ .

#### Lemma 4.5.

Let $f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}$ be a Boolean function. Suppose the input $x$ follows distribution $\Ber(q)^{\otimes n}$ . Consider an algorithm which adaptively makes at most $m$ exact queries in expectation. Let $t\in\{0,1,*\}^{n}$ be the random variable denoting the query results. Then $\mathbb{E}[\I_{q}(f_{t})]\geq\I_{q}(f)-m$ , where $\mathbb{E}$ is over the randomness of the revealed coordinates and the randomness of the algorithm.

#### Proof.

By induction it suffices to prove the case where the algorithm makes exactly one query. Without loss of generality, assume that the algorithm makes an query to coordinate $1$ . Then $t=1*^{n-1}$ with probability $q$ and $t=0*^{n-1}$ with probability $1-q$ .

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\I_{q}(f_{t})] \displaystyle=q\I_{q}(f_{1*^{n-1}})+(1-q)\I_{q}(f_{0*^{n-1}}) \displaystyle=q\sum_{2\leq i\leq n}\Inf_{q,i}(f_{1*^{n-1}})+(1-q)\sum_{2\leq i\leq n}\Inf_{q,i}(f_{0*^{n-1}}) \displaystyle=\sum_{2\leq i\leq n}\Inf_{q,i}(f) \displaystyle=\I_{q}(f)-\Inf_{q,1}(f) \displaystyle\geq\I_{q}(f)-1. $$

The first step is by expanding the expectation. The second step is by definition of $\I_{q}$ . The third step is because $q\Inf_{q,i}(f_{1*^{n-1}})+(1-q)\Inf_{q,i}(f_{0*^{n-1}})=\Inf_{q,i}(f)$ . The fourth step is by definition of $\I_{q}$ . The fifth step is because $\Inf_{q,i}(f)\leq 1$ . ∎

We now apply Lemma 4.5 to Phase 3. Let $t\in\{0,1,*\}^{U}$ be the observations made in Phase 3, where $U=\{i\in[n]:s_{i}=*\}$ is the set of unrevealed coordinates at the end of Phase 2. Then Eq. 10 together with Lemma 4.5 implies that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\rho^{\otimes[n]}}[\mathbb{E}_{t}[\I_{q}((f_{s})_{t})]]\geq(2c-c_{2}\pm o(1))n. $$

#### 4.4.4 Step 3c

After Phase 3, the Boolean function on the unrevealed coordinates has $q$ -biased total influence at least $(2c-c_{2}\pm o(1))n=\Omega(n)$ in expectation. In particular, with probability $\geq c-c_{2}/2\pm o(1)$ , the function has $I_{q}((f_{s})_{t})\geq(c-c_{2}/2\pm o(1))n$ . Any algorithm now needs to output an answer in $\{0,1\}$ . The following result shows that the error probability will be $\Omega(1)$ no matter what the algorithm outputs.

#### Lemma 4.6.

For any $0<c\leq 1$ , there exists $c^{\prime}>0$ such that the following holds. Let $f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}$ be a Boolean function and $\frac{1}{3n}\leq q\leq c/6$ be a parameter. If $\I_{q}(f)\geq cn$ , then

$$ c^{\prime}\leq\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\Ber(q)^{\otimes n}}[f(x)]\leq 1-c^{\prime}. $$

#### Proof.

Since $\I_{q}(f)\geq cn$ and $\Inf_{q,i}(f)\leq 1$ for every $i$ , there exist at least $cn/2$ indices $i\in[n]$ with $\Inf_{q,i}(f)\geq c/2$ . As $\lfloor c/6q\rfloor\leq cn/2$ , there are $m=\lfloor c/6q\rfloor$ indices $i\in[n]$ with $\Inf_{q,i}(f)\geq c/2$ . Without loss of generality, assume that $\Inf_{q,i}(f)\geq c/2$ for $i\in[m]$ .

Let $0^{m}$ denote the length- $m$ bit string with all $0$ ’s. By union bound, we have

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\Ber(q)^{\otimes n}}\left(x_{[m]}=0^{m}\right)\geq 1-\sum_{i\in[m]}\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\Ber(q)^{\otimes n}}\left(x_{i}=1\right)=1-mq\geq 1-c/6.\end{split} $$

Let $\diamond$ denote the concatenation operation of two bit strings. For any $i\in[m]$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle~\mathbb{P}_{y\sim\Ber(q)^{\otimes([n]\backslash[m])}}\left(f(0^{m}\diamond y)\neq f(e_{i}\diamond y)\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle~\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\Ber(q)^{\otimes n}}\left(f(x)\neq f(x\oplus e_{i})\mid x_{[m]}=0^{m}\right) \displaystyle\geq \displaystyle~\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\Ber(q)^{\otimes n}}\left(f(x)\neq f(x\oplus e_{i})\wedge x_{[m]}=0^{m}\right) \displaystyle\geq \displaystyle~\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\Ber(q)^{\otimes n}}\left(f(x)\neq f(x\oplus e_{i})\right)+\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\Ber(q)^{\otimes n}}\left(x_{[m]}=0^{m}\right)-1 \displaystyle\geq \displaystyle\Inf_{q,i}(f)+(1-c/6)-1 \displaystyle\geq \displaystyle~c/3. $$

Finally, we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\Ber(q)^{\otimes n}}(f(x)) \displaystyle\geq\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\Ber(q)^{\otimes n}}(f(x)=1\wedge x_{1}+\cdots+x_{m}=1) \displaystyle=\sum_{i\in[m]}\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\Ber(q)^{\otimes n}}(f(x)=1\wedge x_{[m]}=e_{i}) \displaystyle=q(1-q)^{m-1}\cdot\sum_{i\in[m]}\mathbb{P}_{y\sim\Ber(q)^{\otimes([n]\backslash[m])}}(f(e_{i}\diamond y)=1) \displaystyle\geq\Theta_{c}(q)\cdot\sum_{i\in[m]}\mathbb{P}_{y\sim\Ber(q)^{\otimes([n]\backslash[m])}}(f(0^{m}\diamond y)=0\wedge f(0^{m}\diamond y)\neq f(e_{i}\diamond y)) \displaystyle\geq\Theta_{c}(q)\cdot\sum_{i\in[m]}\left(\mathbb{P}_{y\sim\Ber(q)^{\otimes([n]\backslash[m])}}(f(0^{m}\diamond y)=0)+\mathbb{P}_{y\sim\Ber(q)^{\otimes([n]\backslash[m])}}(f(0^{m}\diamond y)\neq f(e_{i}\diamond y))-1\right) \displaystyle\geq\Theta_{c}(1)\cdot\left(\mathbb{P}_{y\sim\Ber(q)^{\otimes([n]\backslash[m])}}(f(0^{m}\diamond y)=0)+c/3-1\right) \displaystyle\geq\Theta_{c}(1)\cdot\left(\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\Ber(q)^{\otimes n}}(f(x)=0\wedge x_{[m]}=0^{m})+c/3-1\right) \displaystyle\geq\Theta_{c}(1)\cdot\left(\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\Ber(q)^{\otimes n}}(f(x)=0)+(1-c/6)-1+c/3-1\right) \displaystyle=\Theta_{c}(1)\cdot(c/6-\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\Ber(q)^{\otimes n}}(f(x))). $$

Therefore, there exists $c^{\prime}$ depending only on $c$ such that $\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\Ber(q)^{\otimes n}}[f(x)]\geq c^{\prime}$ .

By symmetry, we also have $\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\Ber(q)^{\otimes n}}(f(x))\leq 1-c^{\prime}$ . ∎

Applying Lemma 4.6 to the Boolean function $(f_{s})_{t}$ on the unrevealed coordinates finishes the proof.

## 5 Graph Connectivity

Recall the Graph Connectivity problem, where the input is an unknown undirected graph on $n$ labeled vertices. In each query, the algorithm picks an unordered pair $e=(u,v)\in\binom{V}{2}$ , and the oracle returns whether $e$ is an edge of $G$ , flipped independently with probability $0<p<\frac{1}{2}$ . The goal of the algorithm is to determine whether $G$ is connected or not.

In this section, we prove Theorem 1.2, which we recall below: See 1.2

### 5.1 Preliminaries

#### Lemma 5.1 (Stirling’s formula).

- 1. There exists an absolute constant $\epsilon>0$ such that for all $n\geq 1$ , $\displaystyle\epsilon\sqrt{n}\left(\frac{n}{e}\right)^{n}\leq n!\leq\epsilon^{-1}\sqrt{n}\left(\frac{n}{e}\right)^{n}.$

- 2. Fix $m\geq 2$ . There exists an constant $\epsilon=\epsilon(m)>0$ such that for all $n\geq 1$ and all $k_{1},\ldots,k_{m}\geq 1$ with $k_{1}+\cdots+k_{m}=n$ , $\displaystyle\epsilon\cdot\frac{n^{n+1/2}}{\prod_{i\in[m]}k_{i}^{k_{i}+1/2}}\leq\binom{n}{k_{1},\ldots,k_{m}}\leq\epsilon^{-1}\cdot\frac{n^{n+1/2}}{\prod_{i\in[m]}k_{i}^{k_{i}+1/2}}.$

Let $(\mathbb{P}_{n})_{n}$ and $(\mathbb{Q}_{n})_{n}$ be two sequences of probability measures such that $\mathbb{P}_{n}$ and $\mathbb{Q}_{n}$ are defined on the same measurable spaces $\Omega_{n}$ . We say $\mathbb{Q}_{n}$ is contiguous with respect to $\mathbb{P}_{n}$ , denoted by $\mathbb{Q}_{n}\vartriangleleft\mathbb{P}_{n}$ , if for every sequence $(\mathcal{A}_{n})_{n}$ of measurable sets $\mathcal{A}_{n}\subseteq\Omega_{n}$ , $\mathbb{P}_{n}(\mathcal{A}_{n})\to 0$ implies $\mathbb{Q}_{n}(\mathcal{A}_{n})\to 0$ .

#### Lemma 5.2 (Cayley’s formula).

The number of spanning trees on $n$ labeled vertices is $n^{n-2}$ .

### 5.2 Structure of a uniform spanning tree

Our proof of Theorem 1.2 uses several properties of the uniform random spanning tree (UST) of the complete graph. In this section we state and prove these properties.

The notion of balanced edges is crucial to our construction and analysis.

#### Definition 5.3 (Balanced edges).

Let $\beta>0$ be a constant. Let $T$ be a spanning tree on $n$ labeled vertices. An edge $e\in T$ is called $\beta$ -balanced if both sides of $e$ has at least $\beta n$ vertices. Let $B_{\beta}(T)$ denote the set of $\beta$ -balanced edges of $T$ .

#### Proposition 5.4.

Let $T$ be a UST on $n$ labeled vertices. There exist absolute constants $\epsilon,\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\gamma_{3}>0$ such that with probability at least $\epsilon$ , the following are true simultaneously.

- (i) $\displaystyle\gamma_{1}\sqrt{n}\leq\left|B_{1/3}(T)\right|\leq\gamma_{2}\sqrt{n}.$

- (ii) For all $e\in B_{1/3}(T)$ , if $T_{1}$ , $T_{2}$ are the two connected components of $T\backslash e$ , then $\displaystyle\min\{\left|B_{1/7}(T_{1})\right|,\left|B_{1/7}(T_{2})\right|\}\geq\gamma_{3}\sqrt{n}.$

Our proof of Proposition 5.4 uses the following lemmas.

#### Lemma 5.5 (Balanced edges form a chain).

Let $T$ be a tree on $n$ labeled vertices. Then the subgraph formed by all edges in $B_{1/3}(T)$ is either empty or a chain.

#### Proof.

Suppose $B_{1/3}(T)$ is non-empty. Let $H$ be the subgraph formed by all edges in $B_{1/3}(T)$ .

#### Step 1.

We prove that $H$ is connected. Let $e_{1},e_{2}\in B_{1/3}(T)$ and $e_{3}$ be an edge on the path (in $T$ ) between $e_{1}$ and $e_{2}$ . Let $T_{i,1},T_{i,2}$ ( $i=1,2,3$ ) be the two connected components of $T\backslash e_{i}$ , such that $e_{3}\in T_{1,1}$ , $e_{3}\in T_{2,1}$ , $e_{1}\in T_{3,1}$ , $e_{2}\in T_{3,2}$ . Then $|T_{i,j}|\geq\frac{n}{3}$ for $i,j\in\{1,2\}$ . We have $T_{3,i}\supseteq T_{i,2}$ ( $i=1,2$ ). So $|T_{3,i}|\geq\frac{n}{3}$ for $i=1,2$ and $e_{3}$ is $\frac{1}{3}$ -balanced. This shows that $H$ is connected.

#### Step 2.

We prove that $H$ is a chain. By Step 1, $H$ is a connected subgraph of $T$ , so it is a tree. Suppose $H$ has a vertex $v$ of degree at least three. Then there exist three distinct $\frac{1}{3}$ -balanced edges $e_{1},e_{2},e_{3}$ containing $v$ . Say $e_{i}=(v,u_{i})$ ( $i=1,2,3$ ). Let $T_{i}$ ( $i=1,2,3$ ) be the connected component of $T\backslash e_{i}$ not containing $v$ . Then $|T_{i}|\geq\frac{n}{3}$ and $T_{i}$ ( $i=1,2,3$ ) are all disjoint. This implies

$$ \displaystyle n\geq|T_{1}|+|T_{2}|+|T_{3}|+1\geq n+1, $$

which is a contradiction. So all vertices of $H$ have degree at most two, and $H$ must be a chain. ∎

The following statement about typical distances in a UST is well-known (e.g., [Ald91]).

#### Lemma 5.6 (Typical distance in UST).

Let $T$ be a UST on $n$ labeled vertices and $u,v$ be two fixed vertices (not dependent on $T$ ). Then for any $\epsilon>0$ , there exist absolute constants $\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2}>0$ , such that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left[\gamma_{1}\sqrt{n}\leq\dist_{T}(u,v)\leq\gamma_{2}\sqrt{n}\right]\geq 1-\epsilon, $$

where $\dist_{T}$ denotes the graph distance in $T$ .

To prove Proposition 5.4, we define a probability measure $\mathbb{Q}$ on the space of spanning trees on $n$ labeled vertices that is contiguous with respect to the UST measure, and Proposition 5.4 holds under $\mathbb{Q}$ .

#### Definition 5.7 (Measure $\mathbb{Q}$ ).

We define the measure $\mathbb{Q}$ as follows. A tree tuple $\mathcal{D}$ is a tuple which consists of the following data:

- (i) Six distinct vertices $u_{0},u_{1},u_{2},v_{0},v_{1},v_{2}\in[n]$ .

- (ii) Integers $\frac{n}{3}-\frac{n}{100}\leq L_{0},R_{0}\leq\frac{n}{3}-1$ . Integers $\frac{n}{3}-L_{0}\leq L_{1}\leq\frac{n}{100}$ , $\frac{n}{3}-R_{0}\leq R_{1}\leq\frac{n}{100}$ . Let $W=n-L_{0}-L_{1}-R_{0}-R_{1}$ .

- (iii) A partition of $V=[n]$ into five subsets $V=V_{L_{0}}\sqcup V_{L_{1}}\sqcup V_{R_{0}}\sqcup V_{R_{1}}\sqcup V_{W}$ , where $u_{i}\in V_{L_{i}}$ , $v_{i}\in V_{R_{i}}$ , $u_{2},v_{2}\in V_{W}$ , and $|V_{L_{i}}|=L_{i}$ , $|V_{R_{i}}|=R_{i}$ , $|V_{W}|=W$ ( $i=1,2$ ).

- (iv) Five spanning trees: $T_{L_{i}}$ on $V_{L_{i}}$ , $T_{R_{i}}$ on $V_{R_{i}}$ , $T_{W}$ on $V_{W}$ ( $i=1,2$ ).

Given a tree tuple $\mathcal{D}$ , it produces a spanning tree

$$ \displaystyle T(\mathcal{D})=T_{L_{0}}\cup T_{L_{1}}\cup T_{R_{0}}\cup T_{R_{1}}\cup T_{W}\cup\{(u_{0},u_{1}),(u_{1},u_{2}),(v_{0},v_{1}),(v_{1},v_{2})\}. $$

The measure $\mathbb{Q}$ is the distribution of $T(\mathcal{D})$ , where $\mathcal{D}$ is uniformly chosen from all tree tuples.

#### Lemma 5.8 (Contiguity).

Let $\mathbb{P}$ be the UST measure on $n$ labeled vertices. Let $\mathbb{Q}$ be as defined in Definition 5.7. Then $\mathbb{Q}\vartriangleleft\mathbb{P}$ .

#### Proof.

Let us study the support of $\mathbb{Q}$ . By Lemma 5.5, $\frac{1}{3}$ -balanced edges in $T$ form a chain. By the construction (Definition 5.7), for $T=T(\mathcal{D})$ , $u_{1}$ and $v_{1}$ are the two endpoints of the chain $B_{1/3}(T)$ , and $u_{2}$ (resp. $v_{2}$ ) is the second vertex on the path from $u_{1}$ to $v_{1}$ (resp. $v_{1}$ to $u_{1}$ ). Furthermore, $u_{0}$ (resp. $v_{0}$ ) is the only neighbor $x$ of $u_{1}$ (resp. $v_{1}$ ) not on the path between $u_{1}$ and $v_{1}$ , such that $u_{0}$ ’s connected component in $T\backslash(u_{0},x)$ (resp. $v_{0}$ ’s connected component in $T\backslash(v_{0},x)$ ) has size at least $\frac{n}{3}-\frac{n}{100}$ . This means that $\mathcal{D}$ can be reconstructed given $T(\mathcal{D})$ , up to swapping $(u_{0},u_{1},u_{2})$ and other data with $(v_{0},v_{1},v_{2})$ and the corresponding data. Specifically, every $T$ in the support of $\mathbb{Q}$ is realized by exactly two $\mathcal{D}$ s. Therefore, $\mathbb{Q}$ is equal to the conditional measure $\mathbb{P}(\cdot\mid T\in\supp\mathbb{Q})$ .

Now, to prove that $\mathbb{Q}\vartriangleleft\mathbb{P}$ , it suffices to prove that $\left|\supp\mathbb{Q}\right|=\Theta(\left|\supp\mathbb{P}\right|)=\Theta(n^{n-2})$ . Because every $T$ is realized exactly twice, it suffices to prove that the number of different tree tuples is $\Theta(n^{n-2})$ . We construct a tree tuple according to the following procedure.

- (i) Choose six distinct vertices $u_{0},u_{1},u_{2},v_{0},v_{1},v_{2}\in[n]$ . There are $n!/(n-6)!=\Theta(n^{6})$ ways to do this.

- (ii) Choose $L_{1}$ and $R_{1}$ from $[1,\frac{n}{100}]$ . Choose $L_{0}$ from $\left[\frac{n}{3}-L_{1},\frac{n}{3}-1\right]$ and $R_{0}$ from $\left[\frac{n}{3}-R_{1},\frac{n}{3}-1\right]$ .

- (iii) Choose the partition $V=V_{L_{0}}\sqcup V_{L_{1}}\sqcup V_{R_{0}}\sqcup V_{R_{1}}\sqcup V_{W}$ . There are $\displaystyle\binom{n-6}{L_{0}-1,L_{1}-1,R_{0}-1,R_{1}-1,W-2}$ ways to do this.

- (iv) Choose the five spanning trees, $T_{L_{0}}$ , $T_{L_{1}}$ , $T_{R_{0}}$ , $T_{R_{1}}$ , $T_{W}$ . There are $\displaystyle L_{0}^{L_{0}-2}L_{1}^{L_{1}-2}R_{0}^{R_{0}-2}R_{1}^{R_{1}-2}W^{W-2}$ ways to do this.

Summarizing the above, for large enough $n$ , the number of different tree tuples is

$$ \displaystyle~\frac{n!}{(n-6)!}\cdot\sum_{1\leq L_{1},R_{1}\leq\frac{n}{100}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\frac{n}{3}-L_{1}\leq L_{0}\leq\frac{n}{3}-1\\
\frac{n}{3}-R_{1}\leq R_{0}\leq\frac{n}{3}-1\end{subarray}}\binom{n-6}{L_{0}-1,L_{1}-1,R_{0}-1,R_{1}-1,W-2} \displaystyle~\cdot L_{0}^{L_{0}-2}L_{1}^{L_{1}-2}R_{0}^{R_{0}-2}R_{1}^{R_{1}-2}W^{W-2} \displaystyle\asymp \displaystyle~\sum_{1\leq L_{1},R_{1}\leq\frac{n}{100}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\frac{n}{3}-L_{1}\leq L_{0}\leq\frac{n}{3}-1\\
\frac{n}{3}-R_{1}\leq R_{0}\leq\frac{n}{3}-1\end{subarray}}\binom{n}{L_{0},L_{1},R_{0},R_{1},W}L_{0}^{L_{0}-1}L_{1}^{L_{1}-1}R_{0}^{R_{0}-1}R_{1}^{R_{1}-1}W^{W} \displaystyle\asymp \displaystyle~\sum_{1\leq L_{1},R_{1}\leq\frac{n}{100}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\frac{n}{3}-L_{1}\leq L_{0}\leq\frac{n}{3}-1\\
\frac{n}{3}-R_{1}\leq R_{0}\leq\frac{n}{3}-1\end{subarray}}\frac{n^{n+1/2}}{(L_{0}L_{1}R_{0}R_{1})^{3/2}W^{1/2}} \displaystyle\asymp \displaystyle~\sum_{1\leq L_{1},R_{1}\leq\frac{n}{100}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\frac{n}{3}-L_{1}\leq L_{0}\leq\frac{n}{3}-1\\
\frac{n}{3}-R_{1}\leq R_{0}\leq\frac{n}{3}-1\end{subarray}}\frac{n^{n-3}}{(L_{1}R_{1})^{3/2}} \displaystyle\asymp \displaystyle~\sum_{1\leq L_{1},R_{1}\leq\frac{n}{100}}\frac{n^{n-3}}{(L_{1}R_{1})^{1/2}} \displaystyle\asymp \displaystyle~n^{n-2}. $$

This finishes the proof. ∎

#### Lemma 5.9 (Proposition 5.4, Item (i) for $\mathbb{Q}$ ).

Let $T$ be sampled from $\mathbb{Q}$ (Definition 5.7). For any $\epsilon>0$ , there exist $\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2}>0$ such that with probability at least $1-\epsilon$ , Proposition 5.4, Item (i) holds for $T$ .

#### Proof.

As we discussed in the proof of Lemma 5.8, all edges on the path between $u_{1}$ and $v_{1}$ are $\frac{1}{3}$ -balanced. Conditioned on $V_{W}$ , $T_{W}$ being a UST on $V_{W}$ , by Lemma 5.6,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left[\gamma_{1}\sqrt{W}\leq\dist_{T_{W}}(u_{1},v_{1})\leq\gamma_{2}\sqrt{W}\right]\geq 1-\epsilon. $$

Noting that $\dist_{T}(u_{1},v_{1})=\dist_{T_{W}}(u_{1},v_{1})$ and $W=\Theta(n)$ , we finish the proof. ∎

#### Corollary 5.10 (Proposition 5.4, Item (i)).

Let $T$ be a UST on $n$ labeled vertices. There exist absolute constants $\epsilon,\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2}>0$ such that with probability at least $\epsilon$ , Proposition 5.4, Item (i) holds for $T$ .

#### Proof.

By Lemmas 5.9 and 5.8. ∎

Using Corollary 5.10, we can prove that Proposition 5.4 holds for $\mathbb{Q}$ .

#### Lemma 5.11 (Proposition 5.4 for $\mathbb{Q}$ ).

Let $T$ be sampled from $\mathbb{Q}$ (Definition 5.7). There exist absolute constants $\epsilon,\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\gamma_{3}>0$ such that with probability at least $\epsilon$ , both items in Proposition 5.4 hold for $T$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\mathcal{E}_{L_{0}}$ (resp. $\mathcal{E}_{R_{0}}$ , $\mathcal{E}_{W}$ ) be the event that $\left|B_{1/3}(T_{L_{0}})\right|$ (resp. $\left|B_{1/3}(T_{R_{0}})\right|$ , $\dist_{T_{W}}(u_{1},v_{1})$ ) is in $[\gamma_{1}\sqrt{n},\gamma_{2}\sqrt{n}]$ . Let $\mathcal{E}=\mathcal{E}_{L_{0}}\cap\mathcal{E}_{R_{0}}\cap\mathcal{E}_{W}$ . Let $\mathcal{A}$ be the $\sigma$ -algebra generated by $V_{L_{0}}$ , $V_{R_{0}}$ , $V_{W}$ . Conditioned on $\mathcal{A}$ , the three subtrees $T_{L_{0}}$ , $T_{R_{0}}$ , $T_{W}$ are independent and are USTs on the respective vertex sets. By Lemma 5.6, Corollary 5.10, and $L_{0},R_{0},W=\Theta(n)$ , there exist $\epsilon,\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2}>0$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{L_{0}}|\mathcal{A}),\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{R_{0}}|\mathcal{A}),\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{W}|\mathcal{A})\geq\epsilon^{1/3}. $$

By independence, we have $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}|\mathcal{A})\geq\epsilon$ . Therefore $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E})\geq\epsilon$ .

Now we show that when $\mathcal{E}$ happens, both items in Proposition 5.4 hold. As we discussed in the proof of Lemma 5.8, $B_{1/3}(T)$ is the set of edges on the path between $u_{1}$ and $v_{1}$ . So Item (i) holds because $\mathcal{E}_{W}$ happens. Now consider Item (ii). Let $e$ be an edge on the path between $u_{1}$ and $v_{1}$ . Let $T_{1}$ , $T_{2}$ be the two components of $T\backslash e$ , where $u_{1}\in T_{1}$ , $v_{1}\in T_{2}$ . Then $T_{L_{0}}\subseteq T_{1}$ , $T_{R_{0}}\subseteq T_{2}$ . Every $\frac{1}{3}$ -balanced edge of $T_{L_{0}}$ divides $T_{L_{0}}$ into components of size at least $\frac{|T_{L_{0}}|}{3}$ , so it is a $\beta$ -balanced edge of $T_{1}$ with $\beta=\frac{|T_{L_{0}}|}{3|T_{1}|}\geq\frac{\frac{n}{3}-\frac{n}{100}}{3\cdot\frac{2}{3}n}\geq\frac{1}{7}$ . The same discussion holds for $T_{R_{0}}$ and $T_{2}$ . Because $\mathcal{E}_{L_{0}}$ and $\mathcal{E}_{R_{0}}$ happen, Item (ii) holds. ∎

By Lemmas 5.11 and 5.8, we complete the proof of Proposition 5.4.

#### Lemma 5.12.

Let $T$ be a UST. Then for any $\epsilon>0$ , $0<\beta<\frac{1}{2}$ , there exists $\gamma>0$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left[\left|B_{\beta}(T)\right|\leq\gamma\sqrt{n}\right]\geq 1-\epsilon. $$

#### Proof.

The proof is by the first moment method. Let $e=(u,v)$ be an unordered pair of vertices. For any integer $\beta n\leq k\leq(1-\beta)n$ , the number of spanning trees containing $e$ such that $u$ ’s side contains exactly $k$ (including $u$ ) vertices is

$$ \displaystyle\binom{n-2}{k-1}k^{k-2}(n-k)^{n-k-2}\asymp n^{-2}\binom{n}{k}k^{k-1}(n-k)^{n-k-1}\asymp\frac{n^{n-3/2}}{(k(n-k))^{3/2}}\asymp n^{n-9/2}. $$

So the number of trees $T$ with $e\in B_{\beta}(T)$ is

$$ \displaystyle\asymp\sum_{k\in[\beta n,(1-\beta)n]}n^{n-9/2}\asymp n^{n-7/2}. $$

Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[B_{\beta}(T)\right]\asymp\frac{\binom{n}{2}\cdot n^{n-7/2}}{n^{n-2}}\asymp\sqrt{n}. $$

The result then follows from Markov’s inequality. ∎

#### Lemma 5.13.

Let $T$ be a UST. For $e\in T$ , let $s_{T}(e)$ denote the size of the smaller component of $T\backslash e$ . Then for any $\epsilon>0$ , there exists $\gamma>0$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left[\sum_{e\in T}s_{T}(e)\leq\gamma n^{3/2}\right]\geq 1-\epsilon. $$

#### Proof.

The proof is by first moment method. Let $e=(u,v)$ be an unordered pair of vertices. We define $s_{T}(e)=0$ if $e\not\in T$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[s_{T}(e)\right] \displaystyle\asymp\frac{1}{n^{n-2}}\cdot\sum_{1\leq k\leq\frac{n}{2}}k\cdot\binom{n-2}{k-1}k^{k-2}(n-k)^{n-k-2} \displaystyle\asymp\frac{1}{n^{n}}\sum_{1\leq k\leq\frac{n}{2}}\binom{n}{k}k^{k}(n-k)^{n-k-1} \displaystyle\asymp\sum_{1\leq k\leq\frac{n}{2}}\frac{n^{1/2}}{k^{1/2}(n-k)^{3/2}} \displaystyle\asymp\sum_{1\leq k\leq\frac{n}{2}}\frac{1}{k^{1/2}n} \displaystyle\asymp n^{-1/2}. $$

Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{e\in T}s_{T}(e)\right]\asymp\binom{n}{2}\cdot n^{-1/2}\asymp n^{3/2}. $$

The result then follows from Markov’s inequality. ∎

Combining Proposition 5.4, Lemma 5.12 and Lemma 5.13, we get the following corollary.

#### Corollary 5.14.

Let $T$ be a UST on $n$ labeled vertices. There exist absolute constants $\epsilon,\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\gamma_{3},\gamma_{4},\gamma_{5}>0$ such that the following are true simultaneously.

- (i) $\displaystyle\gamma_{1}\sqrt{n}\leq\left|B_{1/3}(T)\right|\leq\left|B_{1/42}(T)\right|\leq\gamma_{2}\sqrt{n}.$

- (ii) For all $e\in B_{1/3}(T)$ , if $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$ are the two connected components of $T\backslash e$ , then $\displaystyle\gamma_{3}\sqrt{n}\leq\min\{\left|B_{1/7}(T_{1})\right|,\left|B_{1/7}(T_{2})\right|\}\leq\max\{\left|B_{1/14}(T_{1})\right|,\left|B_{1/14}(T_{2})\right|\}\leq\gamma_{4}\sqrt{n}.$

- (iii) $\displaystyle\sum_{e\in T}s_{T}(e)\leq\gamma_{5}n^{3/2}.$

#### Proof.

By Proposition 5.4, there exist $\epsilon,\gamma_{1},\gamma_{3}>0$ such that with probability at least $\epsilon$ , the lower bounds in Corollary 5.14, Items (i) and (ii) hold. By Lemma 5.12, there exists $\gamma_{2}>0$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left[\left|B_{1/42}(T)\right|\leq\gamma_{2}\sqrt{n}\right]\geq 1-\epsilon/3. $$

By Lemma 5.13, there exists $\gamma_{5}>0$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left[\sum_{e\in T}s_{T}(e)\leq\gamma_{5}n^{3/2}\right]\geq 1-\epsilon/3. $$

By union bound, with probability at least $\epsilon/3$ , Corollary 5.14, Items (i) and (iii), and the lower bound in Corollary 5.14, Item (ii) hold. Now notice that $B_{1/14}(T_{1})\cup B_{1/14}(T_{2})\subseteq B_{1/42}(T)$ , so the upper bound in Corollary 5.14, Item (ii) holds with $\gamma_{4}=\gamma_{2}$ . ∎

### 5.3 Hard distribution and three-phase problem

We now start the proof of Theorem 1.2. Our input distribution is defined as follows.

#### Definition 5.15 (Hard distribution for graph connectivity).

Let $\beta_{0}=\frac{1}{21}$ . We generate the input graph $G$ using the following procedure.

- (1) Let $T$ be a UST on vertex set $V=[n]$ .

- (2) If $B_{\beta_{0}}(T)=\emptyset$ , return to the previous step. Otherwise, let $e_{0}\sim\Unif(B_{\beta_{0}}(T))$ .

- (3) Throw a fair coin $z\sim\Ber(1/2)$ . If $z=1$ , output $G=T$ ; if $z=0$ , output $G=T\backslash e_{0}$ .

We define the following three-phase problem, where the algorithm has more power than in the noisy query model.

#### Definition 5.16 (Three-phase problem).

Let $G$ be generated from Definition 5.15. Let $c_{1},c_{2}>0$ be constants to be determined later. Consider the following three-phase problem.

- 1. Phase 1: The algorithm makes $m_{1}=c_{1}\log n$ noisy queries to every unordered pair of vertices $(u,v)\in\binom{V}{2}$ .

- 2. Phase 2: The oracle reveals some edges and non-edges of $G$ . The choice of these edges and non-edges will be described later.

- 3. Phase 3: The algorithm makes up to $m_{2}=c_{2}n^{2}$ (adaptive) exact queries.

The goal of the algorithm is to determine whether the input graph $G$ is connected.

#### Lemma 5.17.

If no algorithm can solve the three-phase problem (Definition 5.16) with error probability $\epsilon>0$ , then no algorithm can solve the graph connectivity problem with error probability $\epsilon$ using at most $m_{1}m_{2}=c_{1}c_{2}n^{2}\log n$ noisy queries.

The proof is similar to Lemma 4.1 and omitted.

#### Proposition 5.18 (Hardness of the three-phase problem).

For some choices of $c_{1}$ , $c_{2}$ , and Phase 2 strategy (Definition 5.16), the following is true: there exists $\epsilon>0$ such that no algorithm can solve the three-phase problem (Definition 5.16) with error probability $\epsilon$ .

#### Proof of Theorem 1.2.

Combining Proposition 5.18 and Lemma 5.17. ∎

The following sections are devoted to the proof of Proposition 5.18.

### 5.4 Phase 1

In Phase 1, the algorithm makes $m_{1}=c_{1}\log n$ noisy queries to every potential edge $e\in\binom{V}{2}$ . Let $a_{e}$ denote the number of times where a query to $e$ returns $1$ . Then for $e\in G$ , $a_{e}\sim\Bin(m_{1},1-p)$ ; for $e\not\in G$ , $a_{e}\sim\Bin(m_{1},p)$ . For $0\leq k\leq m_{1}$ , define

$$ \displaystyle p_{k}=\mathbb{P}(\Bin(m_{1},1-p)=k)=\binom{m_{1}}{k}(1-p)^{k}p^{m_{1}-k}. $$

Let $I=\left[pm_{1}-\log^{0.6}n,pm_{1}+\log^{0.6}n\right]$ .

#### Lemma 5.19.

Let $x\sim\Bin(m_{1},1-p)$ , $y\sim\Bin(m_{1},p)$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(x\in I) \displaystyle=n^{-c_{3}\pm o(1)}, \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(y\in I) \displaystyle=1-o(1), $$

where $c_{3}=c_{1}(1-2p)\log\frac{1-p}{p}$ .

The proof is the same as Lemma 4.3 and omitted.

Let $\mathbb{P}^{(0)}$ denote the graph distribution in Definition 5.15. Let $\mathbb{P}^{(1)}$ denote the posterior distribution of $G$ conditioned on observations in Phase 1. Let $\mathcal{C}^{(0)}$ (resp. $\mathcal{C}^{(1)}$ ) deonte the support of $\mathbb{P}^{(0)}$ (resp. $\mathbb{P}^{(1)}$ ). Then $\mathcal{C}^{(1)}=\mathcal{C}^{(0)}$ and for any graph $H\in\mathcal{C}^{(0)}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{(1)}(H) \displaystyle\propto\mathbb{P}\left((a_{e})_{e\in\binom{V}{2}}|H\right)\mathbb{P}^{(0)}(H), \displaystyle=\left(\prod_{e\in H}p_{a_{e}}\right)\left(\prod_{e\in H^{c}}p_{m_{1}-a_{e}}\right)\mathbb{P}^{(0)}(H). $$

where $H^{c}$ denotes the complement $\binom{V}{2}\backslash H$ .

### 5.5 Phase 2

In Phase 2, the oracle reveals some edges and non-edges of $G$ as follows.

- 2a. In Step 2a, the oracle reveals potential edges $e$ with $a_{e}\not\in I$ .

- 2b. In Step 2b, the oracle reveals every $e\in G$ independently with probability $q_{a_{e}}$ . We choose $q_{j}=1-\frac{p_{m_{1}-j}p_{j_{l}}}{p_{j}p_{m_{1}-j_{l}}}$ for $j\in I$ where $j_{l}=pm_{1}-m_{1}^{0.6}$ .

- 2c. In Step 2c, the oracle reveals $n-2$ edges of $G$ as follows. If $G$ is disconnected, reveal all edges of $G$ . Otherwise, $G$ is connected and is some tree $T$ . If $G$ has a $\beta_{0}$ -balanced edge that is not revealed yet, uniformly randomly choose an edge $e^{*}$ from all such edges, and reveal all edges of $G\backslash e^{*}$ . If all $\beta_{0}$ -balanced edges of $G$ have been revealed, report failure.

#### 5.5.1 Step 2a and Step 2b

By the same analysis as in Sections 4.3.1 and 4.3.2, observations up to Step 2b have the same effect as the following procedure:

#### Definition 5.20 (Alternative observation procedure).

Let $G$ be generated as in Definition 5.15.

- (1) Observe every edge $e\in G$ independently with probability $\displaystyle p_{+}$ $\displaystyle=1-\sum_{j\in I}p_{j}(1-q_{j})=1-\frac{p_{j_{l}}}{p_{m_{1}-j_{l}}}\cdot\sum_{j\in I}p_{m_{1}-j}$ $\displaystyle=1-(1\pm o(1))\frac{p_{j_{l}}}{p_{m_{1}-j_{l}}}=1-n^{-c_{3}\pm o(1)}.$

- (2) Observe every non-edge $e\in G^{c}$ independently with probability $\displaystyle p_{-}=\mathbb{P}(\Bin(m_{1},p)\not\in I)=o(1).$

Let $\mathbb{P}^{(2b)}$ be the posterior distribution of $G$ after Step 2b and $\mathcal{C}^{(2b)}$ be its support. Let $E^{(2a)}_{+}$ (resp. $E^{(2a)}_{-}$ ) denote the set of edges (resp. non-edges) revealed in Step 2a. Let $E^{(2b)}_{+}$ be the set of edges revealed in Step 2b that were not revealed in Step 2a. Define $E^{(\leq 2b)}_{+}=E^{(2a)}_{+}\cup E^{(2b)}_{+}$ . Then $\mathcal{C}^{(2b)}$ is the set of graphs $H\in\mathcal{C}^{(0)}$ satisfying $E^{(\leq 2b)}_{+}\subseteq H$ and $E^{(2a)}_{-}\cap H=\emptyset$ .

By the same analysis as in Sections 4.3.1 and 4.3.2, the posterior distribution satisfies

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{(2b)}(H)\propto\left(\frac{p_{k_{l}}}{p_{m_{1}-k_{l}}}\right)^{|H|-(n-2)}\mathbb{P}^{(0)}(H). $$

for $H\in\mathcal{C}^{(2b)}$ .

#### 5.5.2 Step 2c

Let $E^{(2c)}_{+}$ be the set of edges revealed in Step 2c that were not revealed in previous steps. Let $\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}$ be the posterior distribution of $G$ and $\mathcal{C}^{(2c)}$ be the support of $\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}$ .

#### Lemma 5.21.

Conditioned on $G$ being connected, with probability $\Omega(1)$ , Step 2c does not report failure, and $e^{*}$ is $\frac{1}{3}$ -balanced.

#### Proof.

Step 2c reports failure when $G$ is connected and all $\beta_{0}$ -balanced edges have been revealed in previous steps. Let $T$ be a UST. By Corollary 5.14, for some $\epsilon,\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2}>0$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left[\gamma_{1}\sqrt{n}\leq\left|B_{1/3}(T)\right|\leq\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(T)\right|\leq\gamma_{2}\sqrt{n}\right]>\epsilon. $$

When constructing the input distribution (Definition 5.3), conditioned on $G$ being connected, the distribution of $G$ is uniform over all spanning trees with at least one $\beta_{0}$ -balanced edge. Let $\mathcal{E}_{1}$ be the event that $G$ is connected, has at least $\gamma_{1}\sqrt{n}$ $\frac{1}{3}$ -balanced edges, and at most $\gamma_{2}\sqrt{n}$ $\beta_{0}$ -balanced edges. By the above discussion, $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{E}_{1})=\Omega(1)$ . In Definition 5.20, every edge is observed independently with probability $p_{+}=1-n^{-c_{3}\pm o(1)}$ . By choosing $c_{1}>0$ small enough, we can let $c_{3}>0$ be arbitrarily small. Let $\widetilde{B}_{1/3}$ (resp. $\widetilde{B}_{\beta_{0}}$ ) be the set of $\frac{1}{3}$ -balanced (resp. $\beta_{0}$ -balanced) edges of $G$ not revealed in previous steps. Then

$$ \displaystyle\widetilde{B}_{1/3}\subseteq\widetilde{B}_{\beta_{0}},\qquad\left|\widetilde{B}_{1/3}\right|\sim\Bin\left(\left|B_{1/3}(G)\right|,1-p_{+}\right),\qquad\left|\widetilde{B}_{\beta_{0}}\right|\sim\Bin\left(\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G)\right|,1-p_{+}\right). $$

Note that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\Bin\left(\left|B_{1/3}(G)\right|,1-p_{+}\right)\right] \displaystyle=\left|B_{1/3}(G)\right|\cdot(1-p_{+})=n^{1/2-c_{3}\pm o(1)}, \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\Bin\left(\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G)\right|,1-p_{+}\right)\right] \displaystyle=\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G)\right|\cdot(1-p_{+})=n^{1/2-c_{3}\pm o(1)}. $$

By Bernstein’s inequality, there exists $\gamma_{3},\gamma_{4}>0$ such that conditioned on $\mathcal{E}_{1}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left[\left|\widetilde{B}_{1/3}\right|\geq\gamma_{3}\left|B_{1/3}(G)\right|\cdot(1-p_{+})\mid\mathcal{E}_{1}\right]\geq 1-\exp\left(-n^{1/2-c_{3}\pm o(1)}\right), \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left[\left|\widetilde{B}_{\beta_{0}}\right|\leq\gamma_{4}\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G)\right|\cdot(1-p_{+})\mid\mathcal{E}_{1}\right]\geq 1-\exp\left(-n^{1/2-c_{3}\pm o(1)}\right). $$

Let $\mathcal{E}_{2}$ be the event that $\left|\widetilde{B}_{1/3}\right|\geq\gamma_{3}\left|B_{1/3}(G)\right|\cdot(1-p_{+})$ and $\left|\widetilde{B}_{\beta_{0}}\right|\leq\gamma_{4}\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G)\right|\cdot(1-p_{+})$ . The above discussion shows that $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E}_{2}|\mathcal{E}_{1})=1-o(1)$ .

When $\mathcal{E}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{E}_{2}$ both happen, we have $\frac{\left|\widetilde{B}_{1/3}\right|}{\left|\widetilde{B}_{\beta_{0}}\right|}\geq\frac{\gamma_{3}\gamma_{1}}{\gamma_{4}\gamma_{2}}>0$ . So conditioned on $\mathcal{E}_{1}\cap\mathcal{E}_{2}$ , the probability that $e^{*}$ is $\frac{1}{3}$ -balanced is $\Omega(1)$ . This finishes the proof. ∎

From now on we condition on the event that Step 2c does not report failure, and $e^{*}$ is $\frac{1}{3}$ -balanced. Let us consider the posterior distribution $\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}$ . Let $E^{(\leq 2c)}_{+}=E^{(\leq 2b)}_{+}\cup E^{(2c)}_{+}$ be the set of observed edges at the end of Step 2c. Then $E^{(\leq 2c)}_{+}$ consists of $n-2$ edges, which is a forest with two components $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$ , each containing at least $\frac{n}{3}$ and at most $\frac{2n}{3}$ vertices. The support $\mathcal{C}^{(2c)}$ is easy to describe. Let $G_{0}=T_{1}\cup T_{2}$ and $G_{e}=T_{1}\cup T_{2}\cup\{e\}$ for $e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{C}^{(2c)}=\left\{G_{0}\right\}\cup\left\{G_{e}:e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})\backslash E^{(2a)}_{-}\right\}. $$

The posterior distribution $\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}$ is not simply the distribution $\mathbb{P}^{(2b)}$ restricted to $\mathcal{C}^{(2c)}$ . For $H\in\mathcal{C}^{(2c)}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}(H) \displaystyle\propto\mathbb{P}\left(E^{(2c)}_{+}\mid H,E^{(\leq 2b)}_{+}\right)\mathbb{P}^{(2b)}(H) \displaystyle\propto\mathbb{P}\left(E^{(2c)}_{+}\mid H,E^{(\leq 2b)}_{+}\right)\left(\frac{p_{k_{l}}}{p_{m_{1}-k_{l}}}\right)^{|H|-(n-2)}\mathbb{P}^{(0)}(H). $$

For $H=G_{0}$ , Eq. 18 simplifies to

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}(G_{0})\propto\mathbb{P}^{(0)}(G_{0}). $$

For $H=G_{e}$ , Eq. 18 simplifies to

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}(G_{e})\propto\frac{1}{\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\backslash E^{(\leq 2b)}_{+}\right|}\cdot\frac{p_{k_{l}}}{p_{m_{1}-k_{l}}}\mathbb{P}^{(0)}(G_{e}). $$

Note that the $\propto$ symbols in Eqs. 19 and 20 hide the same factor.

Further simplifying Eqs. 19 and 20, we get

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}(G_{0}) \displaystyle\propto\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})}\frac{1}{\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\right|}, \displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}(G_{e}) \displaystyle\propto\frac{1}{\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\backslash E^{(\leq 2b)}_{+}\right|}\cdot\frac{p_{k_{l}}}{p_{m_{1}-k_{l}}},\qquad\forall e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})\backslash E^{(2a)}_{-}. $$

We now consider the set $B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})$ for $e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})$ . Let $\beta_{1}=\frac{\beta_{0}n}{|T_{1}|}$ , $\beta_{2}=\frac{\beta_{0}n}{|T_{2}|}$ . Then $\frac{1}{14}\leq\beta_{1},\beta_{2}\leq\frac{1}{7}$ and $B_{\beta_{1}}(T_{1})\cup B_{\beta_{2}}(T_{2})\subseteq B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})$ for all $e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})$ . For $e_{i}\in T_{i}$ ( $i=1,2$ ), let $S_{T_{i}}(e_{i})$ be the set of vertices in the smaller component of $T_{i}\backslash e_{i}$ . (If the two components have the same size, choose a side arbitrarily.) For $e=(u_{1},u_{2})\in E(T_{1},T_{2})$ (with $u_{i}\in T_{i}$ , $i=1,2$ ), an edge $e_{i}\in T_{i}\backslash B_{\beta_{i}}(T_{i})$ ( $i=1,2$ ) is in $B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})$ if and only if $u_{i}\in S_{T_{i}}(e_{i})$ . For $i\in\{1,2\}$ and $e=(u_{1},u_{2})\in E(T_{1},T_{2})$ , define

$$ \displaystyle B^{\prime}_{T_{i}}(e)=\{e_{i}:e_{i}\in T_{i}\backslash B_{\beta_{i}}(T_{i}),u_{i}\in S_{T_{i}}(e_{i})\}. $$

Then for $e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})=\{e\}\cup B_{\beta_{1}}(T_{1})\cup B_{\beta_{2}}(T_{2})\cup B^{\prime}_{T_{1}}(e)\cup B^{\prime}_{T_{2}}(e). $$

Note that the union is a disjoint union.

#### Lemma 5.22.

Conditioned on $G$ being connected, there exist constants $\epsilon,\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\gamma_{3}>0$ such that with probability at least $\epsilon$ , the following are true simultaneously.

- (i) Step 2c does not report failure and $e^{*}\in B_{1/3}(G)$ .

- (ii) $\displaystyle\gamma_{1}\sqrt{n}\leq\left|B_{\beta_{1}}(T_{1})\right|+\left|B_{\beta_{2}}(T_{2})\right|\leq\gamma_{2}\sqrt{n}.$

- (iii) $\displaystyle\sum_{e_{1}\in T_{1}\backslash B_{\beta_{1}}(T_{1})}\left|S_{T_{1}}(e_{1})\right|+\sum_{e_{2}\in T_{2}\backslash B_{\beta_{2}}(T_{2})}\left|S_{T_{2}}(e_{2})\right|\leq\gamma_{3}n^{3/2}.$

#### Proof.

Let $T$ be a UST. Let $\mathcal{E}_{1}$ be the event that all items in Corollary 5.14 hold. Then conditioned on $G$ being connected, $\mathcal{E}_{1}$ happens with probability $\Omega(1)$ . In the following, condition on that $G$ is connected and $\mathcal{E}_{1}$ happens.

Let $\mathcal{E}_{2}$ be the event that Lemma 5.22, Item (i) holds. By the proof of Lemma 5.21, conditioned on $\mathcal{E}_{1}$ , $\mathcal{E}_{2}$ happens with probability $\Omega(1)$ . In the following, condition on that $\mathcal{E}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{E}_{2}$ both happen.

By Corollary 5.14, Item (ii), and because $e^{*}\in B_{1/3}(T)$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\left|B_{\beta_{1}}(T_{1})\right|+\left|B_{\beta_{2}}(T_{2})\right| \displaystyle\geq\left|B_{1/7}(T_{1})\right|+\left|B_{1/7}(T_{2})\right|\geq\gamma_{3}\sqrt{n}, \displaystyle\left|B_{\beta_{1}}(T_{1})\right|+\left|B_{\beta_{2}}(T_{2})\right| \displaystyle\leq\left|B_{1/14}(T_{1})\right|+\left|B_{1/14}(T_{2})\right|\leq\gamma_{4}\sqrt{n}. $$

Therefore conditioned on $\mathcal{E}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{E}_{2}$ , Lemma 5.22, Item (ii) holds.

By Corollary 5.14, Item (iii), we have

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{e_{1}\in T_{1}\backslash B_{\beta_{1}}(T_{1})}\left|S_{T_{1}}(e_{1})\right|+\sum_{e_{2}\in T_{2}\backslash B_{\beta_{2}}(T_{2})}\left|S_{T_{2}}(e_{2})\right|\leq\sum_{e\in T}\left|S_{T}(e)\right|\leq\gamma_{5}n^{3/2}. $$

Therefore conditioned on $\mathcal{E}_{1}$ and $\mathcal{E}_{2}$ , Lemma 5.22, Item (iii) holds. ∎

#### Corollary 5.23.

Conditioned on $G$ being connected, there exist constants $\epsilon,\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\gamma_{3},\gamma_{4},\gamma_{5}>0$ such that with probability at least $\epsilon$ , the following are true simultaneously.

- (i) For all $e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})$ , $\displaystyle\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\right|\geq\gamma_{1}\sqrt{n}.$

- (ii) For all $e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})$ , $\displaystyle\gamma_{2}\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\right|\cdot(1-p_{+})\leq\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\backslash E^{(\leq 2b)}_{+}\right|\leq\gamma_{3}\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\right|\cdot(1-p_{+}).$ (24)

- (iii) $\displaystyle\gamma_{4}n^{3/2}\leq\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})}\frac{1}{\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\right|}\leq\gamma_{5}n^{3/2}.$

#### Proof.

Let $T$ be a UST. Let $\mathcal{E}$ be the event that all items in Lemma 5.22 hold. Then conditioned $G$ being connected, $\mathcal{E}$ happens with probability $\Omega(1)$ . In the following, condition on that $G$ is connected and $\mathcal{E}$ happens.

By Lemma 5.22, Item (ii) and Eq. 23, we have

$$ \displaystyle\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\right|\geq\left|B_{\beta_{1}}(T_{1})\right|+\left|B_{\beta_{2}}(T_{2})\right|\geq\gamma_{1}\sqrt{n}. $$

So Corollary 5.23, Item (i) holds. This implies the upper bound in Corollary 5.23, Item (iii) as

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})}\frac{1}{\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\right|}\leq n^{2}\cdot\frac{1}{\gamma_{1}\sqrt{n}}=\gamma_{1}^{-1}n^{3/2}. $$

By Corollary 5.23, Item (i) and Bernstein’s inequality, for every $e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})$ , with probability $1-\exp\left(-n^{1/2-c_{3}\pm o(1)}\right)$ , Eq. 24 holds. By union bound, with probability $1-o(1)$ , Eq. 24 holds for all $e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})$ . This proves Corollary 5.23, Item (ii).

It remains to prove the lower bound in Corollary 5.23, Item (iii). By Lemma 5.22, Items (ii) and (iii), and Eq. 23, we have

$$ \displaystyle~\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})}\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\right| \displaystyle= \displaystyle~\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})}\left(1+\left|B_{\beta_{1}}(T_{1})\right|+\left|B_{\beta_{2}}(T_{2})\right|+\left|B^{\prime}_{T_{1}}(e)\right|+\left|B^{\prime}_{T_{2}}(e)\right|\right) \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle~\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})}\left(1+\gamma_{2}\sqrt{n}+\left|B^{\prime}_{T_{1}}(e)\right|+\left|B^{\prime}_{T_{2}}(e)\right|\right) \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle~(1+\gamma_{2})\sqrt{n}|T_{1}||T_{2}|+\sum_{e_{1}\in T_{1}\backslash B_{\beta_{1}}(T_{1})}\left|S_{T_{1}}(e_{1})\right|\cdot|T_{2}|+\sum_{e_{2}\in T_{2}\backslash B_{\beta_{2}}(T_{2})}\left|S_{T_{2}}(e_{2})\right|\cdot|T_{1}| \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle~(1+\gamma_{2}+\gamma_{3})n^{5/2}. $$

On the other hand, by Cauchy-Schwarz inequality,

$$ \displaystyle\left(\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})}\frac{1}{\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\right|}\right)\left(\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})}\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\right|\right)\geq(|T_{1}||T_{2}|)^{2}\geq\frac{2}{9}n^{2}. $$

So

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})}\frac{1}{\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\right|}\geq\frac{2}{9(\gamma_{2}+\gamma_{3})}n^{3/2}. $$

∎

Now we are able to further utilize Eq. 21 and Eq. 22. Write

$$ \displaystyle Z^{(2c)}=\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})}\frac{1}{\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\right|}+\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})\backslash E^{(2a)}_{-}}\frac{1}{\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\backslash E^{(\leq 2b)}_{+}\right|}\cdot\frac{p_{k_{l}}}{p_{m_{1}-k_{l}}}. $$

Conditioned on that all items in Corollary 5.23 hold, for all $e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})\backslash E^{(2a)}_{-}$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\backslash E^{(\leq 2b)}_{+}\right|}\cdot\frac{p_{k_{l}}}{p_{m_{1}-k_{l}}}\asymp\frac{1}{\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\right|(1-p_{+})}\cdot\frac{p_{k_{l}}}{p_{m_{1}-k_{l}}}\asymp\frac{1}{\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\right|}, $$

where the second step holds because

$$ \displaystyle\frac{p_{m_{1}-k_{l}}}{p_{k_{l}}}\cdot(1-p_{+})=\frac{p_{m_{1}-k_{l}}}{p_{k_{l}}}\cdot\sum_{k\in I}p_{k}(1-q_{k})=\sum_{k\in I}p_{m_{1}-k}=1-p_{-}=1-o(1). $$

Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle Z^{(2c)} \displaystyle\asymp\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})}\frac{1}{\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\right|}\asymp n^{3/2}, \displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}(G_{0}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{Z^{(2c)}}\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})}\frac{1}{\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\right|}\asymp 1. $$

By Bernstein’s inequality, for any $\delta_{1}>0$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left[\left|E^{(2a)}_{-}\right|\geq\delta_{1}n^{2}\right]=o(1). $$

So for small enough $\delta_{1}>0$ , with probability $1-o(1)$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle~\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})\backslash E^{(2a)}_{-}}\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}(G_{e}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle~\frac{1}{Z^{(2c)}}\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})\backslash E^{(2a)}_{-}}\frac{1}{\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\backslash E^{(\leq 2b)}_{+}\right|}\cdot\frac{p_{k_{l}}}{p_{m_{1}-k_{l}}} \displaystyle\asymp \displaystyle~n^{-3/2}\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})\backslash E^{(2a)}_{-}}\frac{1}{\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\right|} \displaystyle\asymp \displaystyle~n^{-3/2}\left(\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})}\frac{1}{\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\right|}-\sum_{e\in E^{(2a)}_{-}}\frac{1}{\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\right|}\right) \displaystyle\asymp \displaystyle~n^{-3/2}\left(n^{3/2}-\delta_{1}n^{2}\cdot n^{-1/2}\right) \displaystyle\asymp \displaystyle~1, $$

where in the second-to-last step we used Corollary 5.23, Items (i) and (iii), and $\left|E^{(2a)}_{-}\right|\leq\delta_{1}n^{2}$ .

Summarizing the above, at the end of Step 2c, with probability $\Omega(1)$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}(\text{disconnected}) \displaystyle=\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}(G_{0})=\Theta(1), \displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}(\text{connected}) \displaystyle=\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})\backslash E^{(2a)}_{-}}\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}(G_{e})=\Theta(1). $$

### 5.6 Phase 3

In Phase 3, the algorithm makes $c_{2}n^{2}$ adaptive exact queries. We show that for $c_{2}>0$ small enough, with probability $\Omega(1)$ , the algorithm will not be able to return the correct answer.

Let $E^{(3)}$ be the set of edges queried in Phase 3. We can w.l.o.g. assume that $E^{(3)}\subseteq E(T_{1},T_{2})\backslash E^{(2a)}_{-}$ , because only queries in this set are useful. Conditioned on $G$ being connected, the probability that $E^{(3)}$ hits the edge $e^{*}$ is

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\sum_{e\in E^{(3)}}\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}(G_{e})}{\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})\backslash E^{(2a)}_{-}}\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}(G_{e})}\leq c_{2}n^{2}\cdot\Theta(n^{-2})\asymp c_{2}, $$

which is $1-\Omega(1)$ for $c_{2}>0$ small enough. Therefore, for small enough $c_{2}$ , with probability $\Omega(1)$ , $E^{(3)}$ does not hit the edge $e^{*}$ .

Conditioned on $E^{(3)}$ does not hit $e^{*}$ , let $\mathbb{P}^{(3)}$ denote the posterior distribution of the original graph $G$ given all observations. We have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{(3)}(\text{disconnected}) \displaystyle=\mathbb{P}^{(3)}(G_{0}), \displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{(3)}(\text{connected}) \displaystyle=\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})\backslash\left(E^{(2a)}_{-}\cup E^{(3)}\right)}\mathbb{P}^{(3)}(G_{e}), $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}(G_{0}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{Z^{(3)}}\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})}\frac{1}{\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\right|}, \displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{(2c)}(G_{e}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{Z^{(3)}}\frac{1}{\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\backslash E^{(\leq 2b)}_{+}\right|}\cdot\frac{p_{k_{l}}}{p_{m_{1}-k_{l}}}, \displaystyle Z^{(3)} \displaystyle=\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})}\frac{1}{\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\right|}+\sum_{e\in E(T_{1},T_{2})\backslash\left(E^{(2a)}_{-}\cup E^{(3)}\right)}\frac{1}{\left|B_{\beta_{0}}(G_{e})\backslash E^{(\leq 2b)}_{+}\right|}\cdot\frac{p_{k_{l}}}{p_{m_{1}-k_{l}}}. $$

By the same discussion as in the end of Phase 2, Step 2c, for $c_{2}>0$ small enough, with probability $\Omega(1)$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{(3)}(\text{disconnected}) \displaystyle=\Theta(1), \displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{(3)}(\text{connected}) \displaystyle=\Theta(1). $$

In this case, any return value would lead to an error probability of $\Omega(1)$ .

This concludes the proof of Proposition 5.18.

### 5.7 $s$ - $t$ Connectivity

In this section we modify the proof of Theorem 1.2 to show hardness of $s$ - $t$ Connectivity. Recall the $s$ - $t$ Connectivity problem, where the input is an unknown undirected graph on $n$ labeled vertices, and a pair of vertices $s,t\in V$ . An algorithm can make noisy queries to edge membership and the goal is to determine whether $s$ and $t$ are in the same connected component of $G$ .

#### Proposition 5.24 (Hardness of $s$ - $t$ Connectivity).

Any algorithm that solves the $s$ - $t$ Connectivity problem with $\frac{1}{3}$ error probability uses $\Omega(n^{2}\log n)$ noisy queries in expectation.

#### Proof.

As discussed in Section 2.2, the error probability in the proposition statement can be replaced with any $0<\epsilon<\frac{1}{2}$ , and the expected number of queries can be replaced with worst-case number of queries.

We design an input distribution for $s$ - $t$ Connectivity by generating $G$ from Definition 5.15, and choosing $s,t$ i.i.d. $\sim\Unif(V)$ .

Then we run the same proof as Theorem 1.2. That is, we define a three-phase problem for $s$ - $t$ Connectivity, where the oracle uses the same strategy in Phase 2 as in Graph Connectivity. Because $s$ and $t$ are independent with $G$ , in the end of Phase 2, conditioned on Step 2c does not report failure, with probability $\Omega(1)$ , $s\in T_{1}$ and $t\in T_{2}$ . In this case, $s$ - $t$ Connectivity is equivalent to Graph Connectivity. In the proof of Graph Connectivity, we have shown that with probability $\Omega(1)$ (over the randomness of the graph and Phase 1 and 2), any algorithm that uses at most $c_{2}n^{2}$ queries in Phase 3 has $\Omega(1)$ error probability. This implies that the same holds for $s$ - $t$ Connectivity. ∎

## 6 Threshold and Counting

In this section we present our proof for Theorem 1.3 and Theorem 1.4. We use $\mathrm{TH}_{k}^{n}$ to denote $k$ -Threshold problem with input length $n$ .

### 6.1 Lower bound for $k$ -Threshold

In this section we prove the lower bound part of Theorem 1.3. That is, solving $\mathrm{TH}_{k}^{n}$ for $k\leq 2n-1$ requires at least $(1-o(1))\frac{n\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}$ noisy queries in expectation. The $k=o(n)$ case has been proved in [WGZW24] (see also Appendix A for our alternative and simpler proof).

#### Theorem 6.1.

For $k=o(n)$ , solving $\mathrm{TH}_{k}^{n}$ with $\delta=o(1)$ error probability requires

$$ (1-o(1))\frac{n\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)} $$

noisy queries in expectation, even when the input is uniformly chosen from $\binom{[n]}{k}$ with probability $1/2$ and uniformly chosen from $\binom{[n]}{k-1}$ with probability $1/2$ .

In our lower bound proof, we will use Theorem 6.1 with $k=O(n/\log n)$ .

We first prove the case where $k=(n+1)/2$ .

#### Lemma 6.2.

Solving $\mathrm{TH}_{k}^{2k-1}$ with $\delta=o(1)$ error probability requires

$$ (1-o(1))\frac{2k\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)} $$

noisy queries in expectation, even when the input is uniformly chosen from $\binom{[2k-1]}{k}$ with probability $1/2$ and uniformly chosen from $\binom{[2k-1]}{k-1}$ with probability $1/2$ .

#### Proof.

Suppose for the sake of contradiction that we have an algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ that solves $\mathrm{TH}_{k}^{2k-1}$ with error probability $\delta=o(1)$ and uses only $(1-\epsilon)\frac{2k\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}$ noisy queries in expectation, for some absolute constant $\epsilon>0$ . Let $\mathcal{D}$ be a distribution of inputs where with $1/2$ probability the input is chosen uniformly from $\binom{[2k-1]}{k}$ , and with $1/2$ probability the input is chosen uniformly from $\binom{[2k-1]}{k-1}$ . Now we consider two cases, depending on whether the expected number of queries $\mathcal{A}$ make on indices with $1$ ’s is larger or not. In either case, we will use $\mathcal{A}$ to obtain an algorithm more efficient than the lower bound in Theorem 6.1, thus reaching a contradiction.

First, suppose $\mathcal{A}$ makes more queries in expectation on indices with $1$ ’s under input distribution $\mathcal{D}$ . Let $k^{\prime}=\Theta(k/\log k)$ and let $n=k-1+k^{\prime}$ . Consider an instance of $\mathrm{TH}_{k^{\prime}}^{n}$ where the input is uniformly chosen from $\binom{[n]}{k^{\prime}}$ with probability $1/2$ and uniformly chosen from $\binom{[n]}{k^{\prime}-1}$ with probability $1/2$ . By Theorem 6.1, this instance requires $(1-o(1))\frac{n\log\frac{k^{\prime}}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}=(1-o(1))\frac{k\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}$ queries in expectation. We will design an algorithm $\mathcal{B}$ solving such an instance utilizing $\mathcal{A}$ .

When $\mathcal{B}$ gets the input, it first adds $2k-1-n$ $1$ ’s to the input, and then randomly shuffle the indices. Then $\mathcal{B}$ sends this input to $\mathcal{A}$ . Whenever $\mathcal{A}$ makes a query to a $1$ that is artificially added, $\mathcal{B}$ simulates a noisy query using random bits; when $\mathcal{A}$ makes a query to an actual input, $\mathcal{B}$ makes a query as well and pass the result to $\mathcal{A}$ . When $\mathcal{A}$ returns a result, $\mathcal{B}$ returns the same result. It is not difficult to verify that the input distribution for $\mathcal{A}$ is exactly $\mathcal{D}$ . Also, whenever the input to $\mathcal{A}$ has at least $k$ $1$ ’s, the input to $\mathcal{B}$ has $k^{\prime}$ $1$ ’s, and vice versa, so the correct output of $\mathcal{A}$ is the same as the correct output of $\mathcal{B}$ . Therefore, $\mathcal{B}$ is correct whenever $\mathcal{A}$ is correct, which happens with probability $\delta$ .

Next, we analyze the expected number of queries $\mathcal{B}$ makes, which consist of two parts:

- • The number of queries $\mathcal{A}$ makes to an actual $0$ in the input: Because we are in the case where $\mathcal{A}$ makes more queries in expectation on indices with $1$ ’s in the input than indices with $0$ ’s, the expected number of this type of queries is at most half of the expected total number of queries $\mathcal{A}$ makes. Thus, the number of queries in this case is at most $(1-\epsilon)\frac{k\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}$ .

- • The number of queries $\mathcal{A}$ makes to an actual $1$ in the input: Each actual $1$ in the input to $\mathcal{B}$ is later permuted to a random position in the sequence. By symmetry, a random $1$ in the input to $\mathcal{A}$ under the input distribution $\mathcal{D}$ is queried at most $\frac{1}{k-1}\cdot(1-\epsilon)\frac{2k\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}$ times in expectation. The number of actual $1$ ’s is $k^{\prime}=\Theta(k/\log k)$ , so the expected number of queries $\mathcal{A}$ makes on them is $\frac{k^{\prime}}{k-1}\cdot(1-\epsilon)\frac{2k\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}=o(1)\cdot\frac{k\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}$ .

As a result, the total number of queries $\mathcal{B}$ makes is $(1-\epsilon)\frac{k\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}$ , which contradicts Theorem 6.1.

For the second case where $\mathcal{A}$ makes more (or equal number of) queries in expectation on indices with $0$ ’s under input distribution $\mathcal{D}$ . The only difference is that, when $\mathcal{B}$ sends the input to $\mathcal{A}$ , it has to flip the roles of $0$ ’s and $1$ ’s. Additionally, it has to flip the result $\mathcal{A}$ returns. We omit the details. ∎

Given Theorem 6.1 and Lemma 6.2, we are ready to prove the lower bound for general $k$ .

#### Theorem 6.3.

Solving $\mathrm{TH}_{k}^{n}$ with $\delta=o(1)$ error probability requires

$$ (1-o(1))\frac{n\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)} $$

noisy queries in expectation for $n/\log n\leq k\leq n/2$ .

#### Proof.

The high-level proof strategy is similar to that of Lemma 6.2, by reducing from a hard instance to $\mathrm{TH}_{k}^{n}$ . However, the difference is that we need to reduce from two different cases depending on whether the average number of queries per $1$ or per $0$ is larger. In Lemma 6.2 we did not have to do it because we can simply flip all the $0$ ’s and $1$ ’s in the input and retain the same problem as $n=2k-1$ .

Let $\mathcal{D}$ be the input distribution where with $1/2$ probability the input is chosen uniformly from $\binom{[n]}{k}$ and with $1/2$ probability the input is chosen uniformly from $\binom{[n]}{k-1}$ . Let $\mathcal{A}$ be an algorithm solving $\mathrm{TH}_{k}^{n}$ under input distribution $\mathcal{D}$ using $(1-\epsilon)\frac{n\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}$ noisy queries in expectation, for some absolute constant $\epsilon>0$ . Let $q_{0}$ denote the expected number of queries $\mathcal{A}$ makes on a random index with input value $0$ (under input distribution $\mathcal{D}$ ), and let $q_{1}$ denote the expected number of queries $\mathcal{A}$ makes on a random index with input value $1$ (under input distribution $\mathcal{D}$ ). Let $Q$ be the expected number of queries $\mathcal{A}$ makes.

Consider the following two cases: $q_{0}\leq q_{1}$ and $q_{0}>q_{1}$ .

#### Case $q_{0}\leq q_{1}$ .

Let $k^{\prime}=\Theta(n/\log n)\leq k$ and let $n^{\prime}=n-k+k^{\prime}$ . Note that $n^{\prime}\in[n/2,n]$ , so we have $k^{\prime}=\Theta(n^{\prime}/\log n^{\prime})$ . By Theorem 6.1, solving $\mathrm{TH}_{k^{\prime}}^{n^{\prime}}$ under input distribution where with $1/2$ probability the input is uniformly from $\binom{[n^{\prime}]}{k^{\prime}}$ and with $1/2$ probability the input is uniformly from $\binom{[n^{\prime}]}{k^{\prime}-1}$ with error probability $\delta$ requires $(1-o(1))\frac{n^{\prime}\log\frac{k^{\prime}}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}=(1-o(1))\frac{n^{\prime}\log\frac{n}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}$ noisy queries in expectation.

Given an instance of $\mathrm{TH}_{k^{\prime}}^{n^{\prime}}$ , we add $n-n^{\prime}$ artificial $1$ ’s to the input, and then randomly permute the input, and feed it to $\mathcal{A}$ . If $\mathcal{A}$ queries an actual input, we also make an actual query; if $\mathcal{A}$ queries an artificial input, we can simulate a query without making an actual query. Finally, we use the result returned by $\mathcal{A}$ as our answer. It is not difficult to verify that this algorithm is correct with error probability $\delta$ , and the input distribution to $\mathcal{A}$ is $\mathcal{D}$ .

Let us analyze the expected number of queries $Q^{\prime}$ used by the algorithm, which can be expressed as follows:

$$ \frac{1}{2}\cdot\left(q_{1}(k^{\prime}-1)+q_{0}(n-k+1)\right)+\frac{1}{2}\cdot\left(q_{1}k^{\prime}+q_{0}(n-k)\right). $$

Also, notice that the number of queries $Q$ made by $\mathcal{A}$ under input $\mathcal{D}$ is

$$ \frac{1}{2}\cdot\left(q_{1}(k-1)+q_{0}(n-k+1)\right)+\frac{1}{2}\cdot\left(q_{1}k+q_{0}(n-k)\right). $$

As $q_{0}\leq q_{1}$ , the above implies that $q_{1}\geq Q/n$ . Furthermore, we have that $Q-Q^{\prime}=q_{1}\cdot(k-k^{\prime})=q_{1}\cdot(n-n^{\prime})\geq\frac{n-n^{\prime}}{n}\cdot Q$ . Therefore,

$$ Q^{\prime}\leq\frac{n^{\prime}}{n}\cdot Q\leq(1-\epsilon)\frac{n^{\prime}\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}\leq(1-\epsilon)\frac{n^{\prime}\log\frac{n}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}, $$

which contradicts Theorem 6.1.

#### Case $q_{0}>q_{1}$ .

By Lemma 6.2, solving $\mathrm{TH}_{k}^{2k-1}$ under input distribution where with $1/2$ probability the input is uniformly from $\binom{[2k-1]}{k}$ and with $1/2$ probability the input is uniformly from $\binom{[2k-1]}{k-1}$ with error probability $\delta$ requires $(1-o(1))\frac{2k\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}=(1-o(1))\frac{2k\log\frac{n}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}$ noisy queries in expectation.

Given such an input to $\mathrm{TH}_{k}^{2k-1}$ , we add $n-2k+1$ artificial $0$ ’s to the input, and then randomly permute the input, and feed it to $\mathcal{A}$ . Similar as before, we make an actual query if $\mathcal{A}$ queries an actual input, and we simulate a query otherwise. It is not difficult to verify that this algorithm is correct with error probability $\delta$ , and the input distribution to $\mathcal{A}$ is $\mathcal{D}$ .

The expected number of actual queries used by the algorithm can be similarly analyzed as the previous case, which can be upper bounded by $(1-\epsilon)\frac{2k\log\frac{n}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)},$ contradicting Lemma 6.2. ∎

### 6.2 Upper bound for $k$ -Threshold

In this section we prove our upper bound for $k$ -Threshold, stated as follows.

#### Theorem 6.4.

Given a sequence $a\in\{0,1\}^{n}$ and an integer $1\leq k\leq n$ , there is an algorithm that can output $\min\{k,\lVert a\rVert_{1}\}$ with error probability $\delta=o(1)$ using

$$ (1+o(1))\frac{n\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)} $$

noisy queries in expectation.

#### 6.2.1 Preliminaries

The following lemmas are standard.

#### Lemma 6.5 (e.g., [GX23, WGZW24]).

For a bit $B$ , there is an algorithm $\textup{{Check-Bit}}(B,\delta)$ that can return the value of the bit with error probability $\leq\delta$ using

$$ (1+o_{1/\delta}(1))\frac{\log\frac{1}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)} $$

noisy queries in expectation.

#### Lemma 6.6 (e.g., [Fel70]).

Consider a biased random walk on $\mathbb{Z}$ starting at $0$ . At each time step, the walk adds $1$ to the current value with probability $p<1/2$ , and adds $-1$ to the current value with probability $1-p$ . Then the probability that the random walk ever reaches some integer $x\geq 0$ is $(p/(1-p))^{x}$ .

#### Lemma 6.7 (e.g., [Fel70]).

Consider a biased random walk on $\mathbb{Z}$ starting at $0$ . At each time step, the walk adds $1$ to the current value with probability $p<1/2$ , and adds $-1$ to the current value with probability $1-p$ . Then the expected number of steps needed to first reach some integer $-x\leq 0$ is $\frac{x}{1-2p}$ .

Our algorithm for $k$ -Threshold and Counting uses the following asymmetric version of Check-Bit.

#### Lemma 6.8.

For a bit $B$ , there is an algorithm $\textup{{Asymmetric-Check-Bit}}(B,\delta_{0},\delta_{1})$ such that:

- • If the actual value of $B$ is $0$ , then the algorithm returns the value of the bit with error probability $\leq\delta_{0}$ using

$$ (1+o_{1/\delta_{1}}(1))\frac{\log\frac{1}{\delta_{1}}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)} $$

noisy queries in expectation.

- • If the actual value of $B$ is $1$ , then the algorithm returns the value of the bit with error probability $\leq\delta_{1}$ using

$$ (1+o_{1/\delta_{0}}(1))\frac{\log\frac{1}{\delta_{0}}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)} $$

noisy queries in expectation.

#### Proof.

Let $a$ and $b$ be two integer parameters to be set later. The algorithm works as follows: we keep querying the input bit, and keep track of the number of queries that returns $1$ (denoted by $q_{1}$ ) and the number of queries that returns $0$ (denoted by $q_{0}$ ). We stop once $q_{1}-q_{0}=-a$ , in which case we declare the bit to be $0$ , or $q_{1}-q_{0}=b$ , in which case we declare the bit to be $1$ .

If the input bit is $1$ , then the probability that the algorithm returns $0$ can be upper bounded by $\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)^{a}$ using Lemma 6.6, so by setting $a=\left\lceil\frac{\log(1/\delta_{1})}{\log((1-p)/p)}\right\rceil$ , this probability is upper bounded by $\delta_{1}$ .

On the other hand, if the input bit is $0$ , then the probability that the algorithm returns $1$ can be upper bounded by $\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)^{b}$ using Lemma 6.6, so by setting $b=\left\lceil\frac{\log(1/\delta_{0})}{\log((1-p)/p)}\right\rceil$ , this probability is upper bounded by $\delta_{0}$ .

Now we consider the expected running time of the algorithm. First suppose the input bit is $1$ , then the algorithm can be viewed as a random walk on integers starting at $0$ , and each time it adds $1$ with probability $1-p$ and subtracts $1$ with probability $p$ . It stops once the random walk reaches $-a$ or $b$ . This stopping time is upper bounded by the first time it reaches $b$ , and the expected number of steps required for it to first reach $b$ is $\frac{b}{1-2p}=(1+o_{1/\delta_{0}}(1))\frac{\log(1/\delta_{0})}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}$ by Lemma 6.7. Similarly, if the input bit is $0$ , then the expected number of queries used by the algorithm is upper bounded by $(1+o_{1/\delta_{1}}(1))\frac{\log(1/\delta_{1})}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}$ . ∎

#### 6.2.2 The proof

We are now ready to state our proof of Theorem 6.4.

Our algorithm is extremely simple and is outlined in Algorithm 1. It repeatedly calls the subroutine $\textsc{Asymmetric-Check-Bit}(a_{i},\delta/2n,\delta/2k)$ from Lemma 6.8 for every $i\in[n]$ , and uses the returned value as the guess for $a_{i}$ . If at any point, the current number of $a_{i}$ whose guess is $1$ reaches $k$ , the algorithm terminates early and return $k$ . Otherwise, the algorithm returns the number of $a_{i}$ whose guess is $1$ at the end.

*Algorithm 1*

```
1: procedure Threshold-Count( $\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\},k,\delta$ )
2: $cnt=0$
3: for $i=1\to n$ do
4: $cnt=cnt+\textsc{Asymmetric-Check-Bit}(a_{i},\delta/2n,\delta/2k)$
5: if $cnt\geq k$ then return $k$
6: return $cnt$
```

#### Error probability.

We first analyze the error probability of the algorithm. First, suppose $\lVert a\rVert_{1}\geq k$ . Let $S\subseteq[n]$ be an arbitrary size- $k$ set where $a_{i}=1$ for $i\in S$ . Then by the guarantee of Asymmetric-Check-Bit, for every $i\in S$ , the probability that the guess for $a_{i}$ is not $1$ is $\leq\delta/2k$ . Therefore, by union bound, the guesses for $a_{i}$ for all $i\in S$ are $1$ with probability $\geq 1-\delta/2$ . Therefore, the count will be at least $k$ so the algorithm will return $k$ as the correct answer with error probability $\leq\delta/2\leq\delta$ .

If $\lVert a\rVert_{1}<k$ , then by union bound, the probability that all guesses are correct is $\geq 1-\frac{\delta}{2k}\cdot\lVert a\rVert_{1}-\frac{\delta}{2n}\cdot(1-\lVert a\rVert_{1})\geq 1-\delta$ , so the returned count of the algorithm is also correct with probability $\geq 1-\delta$ .

#### Expected number of queries.

We first consider the number of $a_{i}$ with $a_{i}=1$ that we pass to Asymmetric-Check-Bit. One trivial upper bound is $\lVert a\rVert_{1}$ . Also, the expected number of $a_{i}=1$ we need to pass to Asymmetric-Check-Bit before $cnt$ is incremented by $1$ is $\leq\frac{1}{1-\delta/2k}$ , so another upper bound is $\frac{k}{1-\delta/2k}\leq(1+o(1))k$ (as $\delta=o(1)$ ). On the other hand, the number of $a_{i}$ where $a_{i}=0$ that we pass to Asymmetric-Check-Bit is upper bounded by $n-\lVert a\rVert_{1}$ . Note that whether we pass some $a_{i}$ to Asymmetric-Check-Bit only depends on the queries we make to $a_{i^{\prime}}$ for $i^{\prime}<i$ , so even given that we pass some $a_{i}$ to Asymmetric-Check-Bit, we can still use the bounds from Lemma 6.8 to bound the expected number of queries we make to $a_{i}$ . Therefore, the expected number of queries can be upper bounded by

$$ (1+o(1))\left(\min\left\{\lVert a\rVert_{1},k\right\}\cdot\frac{\log\frac{n}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}+(n-\lVert a\rVert_{1})\cdot\frac{\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}\right). $$

Then we consider two cases depending on how large $k$ is.

#### Case $k\geq n/\log n$ .

In this case, $\log(n)=(1+o(1))\log k$ , so the expected number of queries can be upper bounded by

$$ \displaystyle(1+o(1))\left(\min\left\{\lVert a\rVert_{1},k\right\}\cdot\frac{\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}+(n-\lVert a\rVert_{1})\cdot\frac{\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle(1+o(1))\frac{n\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}. $$

#### Case $k\leq n/\log n$ .

In this case, $k\log\frac{n}{\delta}=o(n\log\frac{k}{\delta})$ , so the expected number of queries can be upper bounded by

$$ \displaystyle(1+o(1))\left(k\cdot\frac{\log\frac{n}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}+n\cdot\frac{\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle(1+o(1))\frac{n\log\frac{k}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}. $$

### 6.3 Bounds for Counting

Let us first prove a one-sided upper bound for Counting.

#### Theorem 6.9.

Given a sequence $a\in\{0,1\}^{n}$ , there is an algorithm that can output $\lVert a\rVert_{1}$ with error probability $\delta=o(1)$ using

$$ (1+o(1))\frac{n\log\frac{\lVert a\rVert_{1}+1}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)} $$

noisy queries in expectation.

The difference between Theorem 6.9 and the upper bound part of Theorem 1.4 is that we have $\lVert a\rVert_{1}+1$ rather than $\min\{\lVert a\rVert_{1}+1,n-\lVert a\rVert_{1}+1\}$ inside the log term.

#### Proof.

Outlined in Algorithm 2, the algorithm for counting is an adaptation of Algorithm 1. Notice that in Algorithm 1, when calling Asymmetric-Check-Bit, we have $\delta_{0}=\delta/2n$ and $\delta_{1}=\delta/2k$ . The value $\delta_{0}$ is fixed regardless of the value of $k$ , and the value $\delta_{1}$ depends on $k$ . The algorithm for counting in some sense is simulating Algorithm 1, but dynamically adjusting $\delta_{1}$ based on the current estimate of $k$ , which is the number of input bits that are believed to be $1$ ’s.

For simplicity, throughout the analysis, we use $k^{*}=\lVert a\rVert_{1}$ to denote the desired answer. Let $S_{0}\subseteq[n]$ be indices $i$ with $a_{i}=0$ and let $S_{1}=[n]\backslash S_{0}$ .

*Algorithm 2*

```
1: procedure Counting( $\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\},\delta$ )
2: $k\leftarrow 0$
3: $c\leftarrow\{0\}^{n}$
4: $Active\leftarrow[n]$
5: while True do
6: $i^{*}\leftarrow\argmax_{i\in Active}c_{i}$
7: if $c_{i^{*}}\leq-\frac{\log(6(k+1)/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}$ then return $k$
8: if $\textsc{Query}(a_{i^{*}})=1$ then
9: $c_{i^{*}}=c_{i^{*}}+1$
10: if $c_{i^{*}}\geq\frac{\log(6n/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}$ then
11: $Active\leftarrow Active\backslash\{i^{*}\}$
12: $k\leftarrow k+1$
13: else
14: $c_{i^{*}}=c_{i^{*}}-1$
```

#### Error probability.

For any $i$ , we can view the value of $c_{i}$ as a random walk, i.e., after every query to $a_{i}$ , we either adds $1$ to $c_{i}$ or subtracts $1$ from $c_{i}$ . If $c_{i}=1$ , then the probability that we add $1$ to $c_{i}$ after every step is $1-p$ , and the probability that we subtract $1$ is $p$ . If $c_{i}=0$ , then the probability that we add $1$ to $c_{i}$ after every step is $p$ , and the probability that we subtract $1$ is $1-p$ . Conceptually, we can view $c_{i}$ as an infinite random walk, and the algorithm only utilizes some prefix of it.

For $i\in S_{1}$ , by Lemma 6.6, the probability that $c_{i}$ ever reaches $-\left\lceil\frac{\log(6/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}\right\rceil$ is at most

$$ \left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)^{\frac{\log(6/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}}=\delta/6. $$

Furthermore, if some $c_{i}$ never reaches $-\left\lceil\frac{\log(6/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}\right\rceil$ , then $i$ will eventually be removed from $Active$ and contributes towards $k$ . Since the random walks $c_{i}$ ’s are independent for different $i$ ’s, the probability that there are $\lceil k^{*}/2\rceil+1$ many $i\in S_{1}$ where $c_{i}$ reaches $-\left\lceil\frac{\log(6/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}\right\rceil$ can be upper bounded by

$$ \binom{k^{*}}{\lceil k^{*}/2\rceil+1}\cdot(\delta/6)^{\lceil k^{*}/2\rceil+1}\leq 2^{k^{*}}(\delta/6)^{k^{*}/2+1}\leq(1.5\delta)^{k^{*}/2}\cdot(\delta/6)\leq\delta/6, $$

where the last step holds because $\delta=o(1)$ and hence we can assume $1.5\delta\leq 1$ . Thus, up to $\delta/6$ error probability, the number of $i\in S_{1}$ that contributes towards $k$ is at least $k^{*}-(\lceil k^{*}/2\rceil+1)$ , which means the final value of $k$ is $\geq\max\{0,k^{*}-(\lceil k^{*}/2\rceil+1)\}=\max\{0,\lfloor k^{*}/2\rfloor-1\}$ . This further implies that $k+1\geq k^{*}/3$ . Let $E_{1}$ be the event $k+1\geq k^{*}/3$ and as analyzed above, $\mathbb{P}(\neg E_{1})\leq\delta/6$ .

Next, we consider the event $E_{2}$ where all $c_{i}$ for $i\in S_{1}$ never reaches $-\left\lceil\frac{\log(6(k^{*}/3)/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}\right\rceil$ . By Lemma 6.6, the probability that each $c_{i}$ for $i\in S_{1}$ reaches $-\left\lceil\frac{\log(6(k^{*}/3)/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}\right\rceil$ is upper bounded by

$$ \left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)^{\frac{\log(6(k^{*}/3)/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}}=\frac{\delta}{2k^{*}}. $$

Therefore, by union bound, $\mathbb{P}(\neg E_{2})\leq\delta/2$ .

Next, let $E_{3}$ be the event where all $c_{i}$ for $i\in S_{0}$ never reaches $\left\lceil\frac{\log(6n/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}\right\rceil$ . By Lemma 6.6, the probability that each $c_{i}$ for $i\in S_{0}$ reaches $\left\lceil\frac{\log(6n/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}\right\rceil$ is upper bounded by

$$ \left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)^{\frac{\log(6n/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}}=\frac{\delta}{6n}. $$

Therefore, by union bound, $\mathbb{P}(\neg E_{3})\leq\delta/6$ .

Assume $E_{1},E_{2},E_{3}$ all happen. Then we know that $k+1\geq k^{*}/3$ , and so all $i\in S_{1}$ will eventually be removed from $Active$ and contribute towards $k$ . Also, all $i\in S_{0}$ will not contribute towards $k$ . Therefore, the returned value of $k$ will be equal to $k^{*}$ . Hence, the error probability of the algorithm is upper bounded by $\mathbb{P}(\neg E_{1}\vee\neg E_{2}\vee\neg E_{3})\leq\delta/6+\delta/2+\delta/6\leq\delta$ .

#### Expected number of queries.

Next, we analyze the expected number of queries used by the algorithm.

First, for every $i\in S_{1}$ , the expected number of times we query $a_{i}$ is upper bounded by the expected number of steps it takes for the random walk $c_{i}$ takes to reach $\left\lceil\frac{\log(6n/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}\right\rceil$ . By Lemma 6.7, it is bounded by

$$ \frac{\left\lceil\frac{\log(6n/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}\right\rceil}{1-2p}=(1+o(1))\frac{\log\frac{n}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}. $$

Then we consider the expected number of times we query $a_{i}$ for $i\in S_{0}$ . Fix any $i\in S_{0}$ . Let $F_{j}$ be the event where for exactly $j$ distinct $i^{\prime}\in S_{0}\backslash\{i\}$ , the infinite random walk $c_{j}$ ever reaches $\left\lceil\frac{\log(6n/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}\right\rceil$ . By analysis in the error probability part, $\mathbb{P}(F_{j})\leq\binom{n}{j}\cdot(\delta/6n)^{j}\leq\delta^{j}$ . Note that $F_{j}$ is independent with the random walk $c_{i}$ . If $F_{j}$ holds, then the number of times we query $a_{i}$ is upper bounded by the expected number of steps it takes for the random walk $c_{i}$ first hits $\left\lceil\frac{\log(6(k^{*}+j+1))/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}\right\rceil$ (because once $c_{i}$ hits this value, $k$ can never be larger than $k^{*}+j$ under $F_{j}$ , so we will not query $a_{i}$ again). By Lemma 6.7, this expectation is

$$ \frac{\left\lceil\frac{\log(6(k^{*}+j+1))/\delta)}{\log((1-p)/p)}\right\rceil}{1-2p}=(1+o(1))\frac{\log\frac{k^{*}+j+1}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}. $$

Let $Q_{i}$ be the number of times we query $a_{i}$ . Then we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}(Q_{i}) \displaystyle=\sum_{j\geq 0}\mathbb{E}(Q_{i}|F_{j})\cdot\mathbb{P}(F_{j}) \displaystyle\leq\frac{1+o(1)}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}\sum_{j\geq 0}\delta^{j}\cdot\log\left(\frac{k^{*}+j+1}{\delta}\right) \displaystyle\leq\frac{1+o(1)}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}\sum_{j\geq 0}\delta^{j}\cdot\log\left(\frac{(k^{*}+1)(j+1)}{\delta}\right) \displaystyle=\frac{1+o(1)}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}\left(\sum_{j\geq 0}\delta^{j}\cdot\log\left(\frac{k^{*}+1}{\delta}\right)+\sum_{j\geq 0}\delta^{j}\cdot\log(j+1)\right) \displaystyle\leq\frac{1+o(1)}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}\left(\frac{1}{1-\delta}\cdot\log\left(\frac{k^{*}+1}{\delta}\right)+O(1)\right) \displaystyle\leq(1+o(1))\frac{\log\frac{k^{*}+1}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}. $$

Summing up everything, the overall expected number of queries is

$$ (1+o(1))\left(k^{*}\cdot\frac{\log\frac{n}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}+(n-k^{*})\cdot\frac{\log\frac{k^{*}+1}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}\right). $$

Similar to the proof of Theorem 6.4, we consider two cases depending on how large $k^{*}$ is.

#### Case $k^{*}\geq n/\log n$ .

In this case, $\log(n)=(1+o(1))\log(k^{*}+1)$ , so the expected number of queries can be bounded by

$$ \displaystyle(1+o(1))\left(k^{*}\cdot\frac{\log\frac{k^{*}+1}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}+(n-k^{*})\cdot\frac{\log\frac{k^{*}+1}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle(1+o(1))\frac{n\log\frac{k^{*}+1}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}. $$

#### Case $k^{*}\leq n/\log n$ .

In this case, $k^{*}\log\frac{n}{\delta}=o(n\log\frac{k^{*}+1}{\delta})$ , so the expected number of queries can be bounded by

$$ \displaystyle(1+o(1))\left(k^{*}\cdot\frac{\log\frac{n}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}+n\cdot\frac{\log\frac{k^{*}+1}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle(1+o(1))\frac{n\log\frac{k^{*}+1}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}. $$

∎

Finally, we prove Theorem 1.4, which we recall below:

See 1.4

#### Proof.

Suppose there is an algorithm for Counting with

$$ (1-\epsilon)\frac{n\log\frac{\min\{\lVert a\rVert_{1},n-\lVert a\rVert_{1}\}+1}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)} $$

noisy queries in expectation, for some absolute constant $c>0$ . First, suppose $\lVert a\rVert_{1}\leq n/2$ . Recall that in the lower bound for $k$ -Threshold, the hard distribution for $k$ -Threshold is to distinguish whether the input contains $k$ or $k-1$ $1$ ’s. Thus, by running the assumed algorithm for Counting, the running time would be

$$ (1-\epsilon)\frac{n\log\frac{k+1}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}, $$

which contradicts the lower bound for $k$ -Threshold.

If $\lVert a\rVert_{1}>n/2$ , we can simply first flip all the bits in the $k$ -Threshold instance, and then use the same argument.

For the upper bound, given Theorem 6.9, it suffices to first estimate whether $\lVert a\rVert_{1}$ is bigger than $n/2$ or smaller. When it is smaller, we can directly run Theorem 6.9; otherwise, we first flip all input bits and then run Theorem 6.9.

More precisely, we randomly sample $n^{0.99}$ input elements with replacements, use Lemma 6.5 to estimate them with error probability $1/n^{100}$ . If the fraction of elements in the sample whose estimates are $1$ is $\leq\frac{1}{2}$ , we directly call Theorem 6.9 with error bound $\delta$ and return the result; otherwise, we flip all input bits, call Theorem 6.9 with error bound $\delta$ , and return $n$ minus the result.

Regardless of whether we flip the input bits, the output is always correct assuming the returned result of Theorem 6.9 is correct. Therefore, the error probability of the algorithm is at most $\delta$ .

Next, we analyze the expected running time of the algorithm. Let $E_{1}$ be the event that the fraction of sampled elements that are $1$ is within $n^{-0.01}$ of the fraction of all elements that are $1$ . By Chernoff bound,

$$ \mathbb{P}(\neg E_{1})\leq 2e^{-2\left(n^{-0.01}\right)^{2}\cdot n^{0.99}}\leq O\left(\frac{1}{n^{99}}\right). $$

Let $E_{2}$ be the event that the returned result of Lemma 6.5 for all sampled elements are correct. By union bound,

$$ \mathbb{P}(\neg E_{2})\leq\frac{1}{n^{99}}. $$

If $E_{1}$ and $E_{2}$ both hold, the expected number of queries of Theorem 6.9 can be bounded as

$$ (1+o(1))\cdot\frac{n}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}\cdot\begin{cases}\log\frac{\lVert a\rVert_{1}+1}{\delta},&\text{if }\lVert a\rVert_{1}\leq n/2-n^{0.99},\\
\log\frac{n+1}{\delta},&\text{if }n/2-n^{0.99}<\lVert a\rVert_{1}\leq n/2+n^{0.99},\\
\log\frac{n-\lVert a\rVert_{1}+1}{\delta},&\text{if }\lVert a\rVert_{1}>n/2+n^{0.99}.\end{cases} $$

Regardless of which case it is, the expected number of queries is always $(1+o(1))\frac{n\log\frac{\min\{\lVert a\rVert_{1},n-\lVert a\rVert_{1}\}+1}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}$ . Even if $E_{1}$ and $E_{2}$ do not both hold, the expected number of queries of Theorem 6.9 can be bounded as

$$ (1+o(1))\cdot\frac{n\log\frac{n+1}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}. $$

Therefore, the overall expected number of queries can be bounded as

$$ \displaystyle n^{0.99}\cdot(1+o(1))\cdot\frac{\log\frac{1}{n^{100}}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)}+(1+o(1))\frac{n\log\frac{\min\{\lVert a\rVert_{1},n-\lVert a\rVert_{1}\}+1}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)} \displaystyle+\mathbb{P}(\neg E_{1}\vee\neg E_{2})(1+o(1))\frac{n\log\frac{n+1}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)} \displaystyle= \displaystyle(1+o(1))\frac{n\log\frac{\min\{\lVert a\rVert_{1},n-\lVert a\rVert_{1}\}+1}{\delta}}{D_{\KL}(p\parallel 1-p)} $$

as desired. ∎
